course.title: SQL: From Rows to Reports
course.description: Read a table, compare queries, and build reports with joins, groups and windows.
course.audience: An adult beginning SQL; arithmetic and familiarity with rows and columns are sufficient.

paragraphs: A table of orders with six rows can be read at a glance, but a table of six million cannot, and most of the information that shops, schools and hospitals keep lives in tables of that second kind. SQL is the language for putting a question to such a table. A query of a few lines can find the largest order, list the customers who have never bought anything or set this month's sales beside last month's, and the database works out the answer in the same way whether the table holds six rows or six million.

What makes SQL worth learning carefully is that a query can run without complaint and still answer a different question from the one you meant. An average can be divided by fewer rows than you expected because some values are missing, a join can repeat a customer once for every order or drop a customer who has none, and a result cut to its first ten rows can keep different rows on different runs. Each of these follows from a precise rule, and once you know the rules you can read a query and say exactly which rows it returns and what each number in its result is counting.
outcomes: You'll be able to say what one row of a table stands for, and how a table tells its rows apart.
You'll be able to read a query and say exactly which rows and columns it returns.
You'll be able to summarise rows with counts, totals and averages, and say how missing values affect them.
You'll be able to follow a join between two tables and know which rows it keeps or drops.
You'll be able to rank rows, and work out running totals, without losing any rows.
introduction.prerequisites: You should be comfortable with everyday arithmetic and with reading rows and columns in a spreadsheet; no SQL is assumed.

lessons.title: Know what a row represents

lead.text: A **table** stores its data in rows and columns. In the `customers` table shown here, each **row** is one customer and each **column** holds one fact that is recorded for every customer: an id, a name and a region.
The two queries differ only in the columns they ask for. Switch between them and count the rows each one returns.

afterFigure.text: Both queries return four rows, because choosing columns changes how much is shown about each customer and leaves the number of customers alone. The number of rows in a result comes from **what a row stands for** and from which rows are kept.
For `customers` the answer is a person, so four rows means four customers.

queries.label: All three columns
queries.sql: SELECT id, name, region FROM customers ORDER BY id;

queries.label: The name column only
queries.sql: SELECT name FROM customers ORDER BY id;

lead.text: The shop keeps a second table, `orders`, with one row for each order. Several of its columns repeat: the figure shows that the `item` column holds Desk, Book and Lamp twice each, so knowing that an order was for a desk does not tell you *which* order is meant. The `id` column behaves differently, because **every order has a number of its own**.

A column whose values are different in every row, and which is used to identify the rows, is called the table's **primary key**. SQLite, the database program that runs the queries in this course, will refuse to store a second row with a key that already exists, and that refusal is what lets a query rely on the key to name *exactly* one row.

afterFigure.text: The key also tells you what the table is about: the ids 101 to 106 name orders, so each row is an order. When you meet an unfamiliar table, **the column that cannot repeat** is the quickest way to find out what its rows stand for.

queries.label: Items
queries.sql: SELECT item FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Order ids
queries.sql: SELECT id FROM orders ORDER BY id;

lead.text: The `orders` table also has a column called `customer_id`, and it does not hold a number that *belongs to the order*. It holds the id of the customer who placed the order, so the 2 in orders 103 and 104 means Ben, whose id in the `customers` table is 2. A column that stores the [[primary key|A column whose values never repeat, so each value picks out one row. Met in 'Know what a row represents'.]] of a row in another table is called a **foreign key**.
Because one customer can place several orders, the same `customer_id` can appear in several rows of `orders`. **That repetition is harmless**, since the order id still tells the rows apart.

queries.label: Orders, with a customer id
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, item, amount FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Customers, with their own id
queries.sql: SELECT id, name, region FROM customers ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Customers: id and name
queries.sql: SELECT id, name FROM customers ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Orders: id and customer id
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Orders for customer 1
queries.sql: SELECT id, item FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Orders for customer 2
queries.sql: SELECT id, item FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 2 ORDER BY id;

lead.text: Order 106 is a lamp whose amount nobody has recorded yet. The table could store 0 in that cell, but 0 would say that the order cost nothing, and an unknown price is **not the same fact** as a price of nothing. SQL therefore has a special marker, **NULL**, which means that the value is *missing* or unknown.
A cell that holds `NULL` does not match *any* test for a number, so a query has to ask for it with its own wording, `IS NULL`, and the rows with a known amount are found with `IS NOT NULL`.

queries.label: The amount is missing
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NULL ORDER BY id;

queries.label: The amount is known
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY id;

lead.text: When Cy places another order, the shop adds one row to `orders` and leaves `customers` untouched, because Cy was *already* there and nothing about Cy has changed. The new row carries Cy's id in its `customer_id` column, which is how the order finds its way back to Cy.

A person who signs up creates a customer, so the new row goes into `customers`, and `orders` gains nothing until that person buys something. A customer with no orders is therefore **a perfectly ordinary state of the data**.

afterFigure.text: **Rows in customers count people and rows in orders count purchases**, so a person with no purchases adds to the first count and to nothing in the second.

lessons.orientation: What a row stands for decides what every count over a table is counting, and a primary key and NULL are how a table identifies its rows and records what is missing.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: Take the query `SELECT name FROM customers`. On the shop's `customers` table it returns four names, one for each person who has signed up. On a table that holds one row for each sale, Ada would appear twice if she had bought twice, and counting the rows would count *purchases* instead of *people*.
The two queries are identical and their answers mean different things, because **what a single row stands for** decides what every count, total and average over the table is really counting.

intro.promise: By the end you'll say what one row of a table stands for, find the column that tells rows apart, and keep a missing value separate from zero.

recap.keyIdea: A row stands for one thing, a primary key tells the rows apart, and `NULL` marks a value that is missing.

blocks.text: The first question to ask of a table is what one of its rows represents, since that decides what a count of rows is counting. A **primary key** such as the order id never repeats, so it names exactly one row, while a [[foreign key|A column that holds the key of a row in another table, so its values may repeat. Met in 'Know what a row represents'.]] such as `customer_id` refers to a row in another table and may repeat.

A value that is unknown is stored as **NULL** and not as 0, because zero is a price and `NULL` is the absence of one. Keeping that difference in mind is what lets a later query count, total and average *honestly*.

recap.nextHook: So far every query has returned the columns of one table as they are stored. Next you'll choose which columns appear, rename them, and calculate new ones, without changing the table itself.

lessons.title: Choose the columns you need

lead.text: A **query** is a question put to a table, and its first part, **SELECT**, lists the columns that the answer should contain, in the order in which they are written. The first query in the figure writes `SELECT *`, where the star stands for every column, so its result repeats all six columns of the `orders` table. The second names two of them, so each row of its result holds just an id and an item. The words `FROM orders` say which table to read, and `ORDER BY id` at the end keeps the rows in the order of their ids.

afterFigure.text: Both results have six rows, because choosing columns has *no* effect on which rows appear. That is also why **naming the columns you need** is better than writing the star: the result then says exactly what it contains.

queries.label: Every column
queries.sql: SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Id and item only
queries.sql: SELECT id, item FROM orders ORDER BY id;

lead.text: A [[query|A question put to a table, written in SQL. Met earlier in 'Choose the columns you need'.]] **reads the stored table and builds a new, temporary table** from it for the answer, so leaving out a column from the answer leaves it in the data. Nothing the query does can *delete* the `amount` column or *change* a value in it.
This is what lets many different queries read the same table without interfering with one another.

afterFigure.text: If a stored value is wrong, the fix has to be made in the table itself, since no choice of columns in a query will correct it.

lead.text: The same separation holds outside SQL, wherever one document is built from another.

The heading of a result column is normally the name of the column it came from, and that name may not suit the report. The `orders` table stores a number in a column called `amount`, but a reader of the result might expect to see `price`. Writing `AS` after a column gives it another name for the length of the query, and that new name is called an **alias**.

afterFigure.text: The alias exists **only in the result**, so a later query that reads the table must say `amount` and not `price`. Aliases are most useful once a query calculates a value, because a calculated column has no stored name to borrow.

queries.label: Without AS
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: With AS
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount AS price FROM orders ORDER BY id;

lead.text: In place of a column name, the `SELECT` list can hold an **expression**, a calculation built from columns, numbers and operators such as `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`, which the query works out separately for *each row*. In the second query of the figure, `amount / 2 AS half` halves the amount in every row and uses `AS` to give the new column an [[alias|A name a query gives a result column, written with AS. Met earlier in 'Choose the columns you need'.]].
Order 106, whose amount is unknown, gives an unknown result, because half of a value that nobody knows is still not known, so **NULL is carried through the calculation**.

queries.label: The stored amounts
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Half of each amount
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount / 2 AS half FROM orders ORDER BY id;

lessons.orientation: Use SELECT to choose the columns of a result, AS to rename them and expressions to calculate new values, while the stored table stays as it was.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: The orders table has six columns, yet the query `SELECT id, item FROM orders` returns only two of them. Nothing in the table has been removed or altered, because the query describes the answer it wants and the table it reads stays *exactly* as it was.
Because a query only describes its answer, one table can serve many different questions, each choosing **which facts about each row the answer needs** and leaving the rest where they are stored.

intro.promise: By the end you'll write a SELECT list that returns the columns you need, give a result column a clearer heading, and calculate a new value for each row.

recap.keyIdea: `SELECT` chooses the columns of a result, `AS` renames one, and an expression calculates a new value for every row, while the stored table stays unchanged.

blocks.text: A **query** returns only the columns its `SELECT` list names, so the result can be *narrower* than the table and the stored data is left alone. An **alias** written with `AS` changes a heading in the result and nothing more, and an **expression** such as `amount * 3` is worked out separately for each row.

A calculation on a missing value gives a missing value, so a missing amount stays [[NULL|A marker for a value that is missing or unknown, not the same as zero. Met in 'Know what a row represents'.]] after it has been halved, doubled or increased. Knowing exactly which rows and columns a result contains is what lets you choose which of them to keep.

recap.nextHook: Every query so far has returned a row for each order. Next you'll write conditions that keep only the rows a question needs.

lessons.title: Write the condition you mean

lead.text: After the word `WHERE` comes a **condition**, a test that is applied to every row separately and comes out true or false, and **a row that fails is left out of the result altogether**. The symbols are the ones from arithmetic, `=`, `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`, with `<>` for "is not equal to".

afterFigure.text: The two queries differ by one symbol and by two rows, because orders 102 and 105 have an amount of exactly 20. The symbol `>=` **keeps a row that sits on the limit** and the symbol `>` does not, so choosing between them is choosing what happens *on* the line.

queries.label: At least 20
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount >= 20 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: More than 20
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount > 20 ORDER BY id;

lead.text: A sign in a bookshop uses the same kind of test as a condition, applied to each book on the shelf in turn.

The first query in the figure asks for `amount <= 40` and returns three orders, yet order 106 is absent, although a missing amount could be small. Comparing an unknown value with a number gives neither true nor false but *unknown*, and **a row is kept only when its condition is true**. The comparison is unknown even for `amount = NULL`, because the left side is not known, so that condition keeps no row at all and produces no warning.

To find the row, you ask about the missing value itself. The condition `amount IS NULL` is true only where the amount is missing, which is order 106, and **amount IS NOT NULL** is true wherever an amount is stored.

afterFigure.text: The second and third queries split the table cleanly, with one order in the first group and five in the second. Whenever a column can hold [[NULL|A marker for a value that is missing or unknown, not the same as zero. Met in 'Know what a row represents'.]], a condition on it has to decide what should happen to the rows where it does.

queries.label: Amount at most 40
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount <= 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Amount is missing
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NULL ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Amount is known
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY id;

queries.label: At least 40
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: At least 80
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount >= 80 ORDER BY id;

lead.text: Two conditions can be joined into one. With **AND** a row is kept only when both conditions are true for it, and with **OR** it is kept when at least one is. Text is compared in the same way as numbers, but the value is written in single quotes, as in `item = 'Lamp'`.

In the first query of the figure only order 104 is both a lamp and worth at least 40, since the other lamp has *no* amount. In the second query a row needs to pass only one of the two tests, so order 106 passes because it is a lamp, even though its amount is unknown, since the other condition is already true.

afterFigure.text: `AND` *narrows* a result and `OR` *widens* it. When a question says "both", it needs `AND`, and when it says "either", it needs `OR`.

queries.label: Lamp AND at least 40
queries.sql: SELECT id, item, amount FROM orders WHERE item = 'Lamp' AND amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Lamp OR at least 40
queries.sql: SELECT id, item, amount FROM orders WHERE item = 'Lamp' OR amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Both conditions
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, status FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' AND amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Either condition
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, status FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' OR amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

lead.text: A range is a common thing to ask for, and SQL has a word for it. The condition `amount BETWEEN 20 AND 40` is shorthand for **amount >= 20 AND amount <= 40**, which means that an amount of exactly 20 and an amount of exactly 40 *both* pass.

The figure sets it beside a version written with strict symbols, `> 20 AND < 40`, which leaves both ends out and returns no rows at all, since none of the stored amounts lies strictly between 20 and 40.

afterFigure.text: **An empty result is a legitimate answer** and not an error. Whenever you read a range, check whether each end is counted.

queries.label: BETWEEN, ends counted
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount BETWEEN 20 AND 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Strict symbols, ends left out
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount > 20 AND amount < 40 ORDER BY id;

lead.text: The condition `item IN ('Desk', 'Lamp')` is true when the item equals **any value in the list**, so it means the same as `item = 'Desk' OR item = 'Lamp'` and stays short however long the list grows.
Each query keeps every order whose item appears in its list, so a list of two items can match *more* than two rows, because several orders may be for the same item.

queries.label: Desk or Lamp
queries.sql: SELECT id, item FROM orders WHERE item IN ('Desk', 'Lamp') ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Desk or Book
queries.sql: SELECT id, item FROM orders WHERE item IN ('Desk', 'Book') ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Book or Lamp
queries.sql: SELECT id, item FROM orders WHERE item IN ('Book', 'Lamp') ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Missing amount
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NULL ORDER BY id;

lessons.orientation: Use a WHERE condition to keep exactly the rows a question needs, including the rows on a boundary and the rows where a value is missing.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: The query `SELECT id, amount FROM orders` returns every order, but a question about a shop is usually about the orders worth at least 20, or the ones still pending, and a query says which rows it means with a `WHERE` clause such as `WHERE amount >= 20`.
A clause like this is easy to write slightly wrong, because **one symbol decides whether an order of exactly 20 is kept** and a missing amount behaves differently from every number.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read a condition as a test on each row, join conditions with AND and OR, and say exactly which rows pass at a boundary or when a value is missing.

recap.keyIdea: A condition is a test that each row passes or fails, and it must be written so that its boundaries and its missing values do what the question means.

blocks.text: A **condition** after `WHERE` is applied to every row separately, and only the rows for which it is true are kept. `AND` needs both conditions, `OR` needs either, `BETWEEN` counts both of its ends, and `IN` checks a value against a list.

A comparison with a missing value is neither true nor false, so the row fails it, and a missing value has to be asked for with **IS NULL**. Before you trust a condition, test it on the rows that sit *exactly* on the limit and on the rows where a value is missing.

recap.nextHook: A condition decides which rows are kept, but the kept rows still arrive in no promised order. Next you'll put them in order and keep only the first few.

lessons.title: Make the first row meaningful

lead.text: A query that says nothing about order promises nothing about it. The rows may well arrive in the order in which they were stored, but that is a habit of the database and *not a rule*. To fix the order you add **ORDER BY** and name the column to sort by, followed by **ASC** for ascending, with the smallest value first, or **DESC** for descending, with the largest first.

afterFigure.text: `ORDER BY` never adds or removes a row, and the order it creates is **a promise that you can rely on**.

queries.label: Smallest id first
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders ORDER BY id ASC;

queries.label: Largest id first
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders ORDER BY id DESC;

lead.text: A report often needs only the top of a list, such as the three largest orders. **LIMIT** followed by a number keeps that many rows from the start of the result and drops the rest, which makes the order essential: `LIMIT 2` over an unordered result keeps two rows that *nobody chose*.
`WHERE amount IS NOT NULL` leaves out order 106, because SQLite treats a missing value as smaller than any number and it would otherwise head an ascending list.

afterFigure.text: **LIMIT is a maximum and not a promise**: if fewer rows are available than the limit allows, the query simply returns what exists.

queries.label: The two smallest amounts
queries.sql: SELECT amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount ASC LIMIT 2;

queries.label: The four smallest amounts
queries.sql: SELECT amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount ASC LIMIT 4;

lead.text: A race result works like a sorted list that is cut short by a limit.

Two orders can have the same amount, and `ORDER BY amount` alone does not say which of them comes first. In the figure the amount 20 belongs to orders 102 and 105, and the amount 80 to orders 101 and 103. **A database may place such rows in either order**, and a different run of the same query may place them differently.

The remedy is a second sort column, which is consulted *only* when the first one ties. `ORDER BY amount ASC, id ASC` sorts by amount and, among equal amounts, by id, and because a [[primary key|A column whose values never repeat, so each value picks out one row. Met in 'Know what a row represents'.]] never repeats, the order is then decided completely. The second query reverses the tie-breaker alone, and the tied pairs swap places while everything else stays still.

afterFigure.text: A tie-breaker matters most when a limit is applied, because a tie at the cut-off decides which row is kept. **Ending every important ORDER BY with a unique column** removes that doubt.

queries.label: Lower id first among ties
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount ASC, id ASC;

queries.label: Higher id first among ties
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount ASC, id DESC;

queries.label: Ties broken by lower id
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

queries.label: Ties broken by higher id
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id DESC;

lead.text: When a query has a `WHERE` clause, an `ORDER BY` and a `LIMIT`, they act in that sequence. **WHERE decides which rows exist, ORDER BY arranges them, and LIMIT takes the first few** of the arranged rows. A limit therefore keeps the first rows of the *filtered* list, and the question being asked is decided by the filter as much as by the sort.

The first query in the figure asks for the smallest pending order with a known amount, and it returns order 104 with 40, although a paid order with an amount of 20 is smaller, because the paid orders were removed before the sorting began.

afterFigure.text: Reading a query in this order, **filter then sort then limit**, is the reliable way to say what it returns.

queries.label: Smallest pending order
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending' AND amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount ASC, id ASC LIMIT 1;

queries.label: Largest desk
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE item = 'Desk' ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC LIMIT 1;

lessons.orientation: Use ORDER BY to give a result a promised order, and LIMIT with a tie-breaker to keep exactly the rows you mean.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: A table is a collection of rows with no built-in sequence, so it has no first row. A query that says `ORDER BY amount DESC LIMIT 1` does return the order with the largest amount, but only if no two orders share that amount, and in the shop's table two of them do.

A limited result is useful only when its order is fully decided, because **the order determines which rows survive the cut**. To get the largest order, or the three smallest, reliably, a query has to say how to sort and how to break a tie between equal amounts.

intro.promise: By the end you'll sort a result in either direction, break ties so that a limit keeps the rows you intend, and say which rows a filtered, sorted and limited query returns.

recap.keyIdea: `ORDER BY` gives a result a promised order, and `LIMIT` keeps the first rows of it, so a tie-breaker is needed whenever a tie could decide which rows are kept.

blocks.text: Without **ORDER BY** a query promises no order, and **LIMIT** keeps the first rows of whatever order it has, so the two belong together. A second sort column, ideally a unique one such as the [[primary key|A column whose values never repeat, so each value picks out one row. Met in 'Know what a row represents'.]], breaks ties so that the *same* rows are kept on every run.

The parts of a query act in a fixed sequence: `WHERE` filters the rows, `ORDER BY` arranges those that remain, and `LIMIT` takes the first few. Reading a query in that sequence tells you exactly which rows it returns.

recap.nextHook: Sorting and limiting keep every kept row, repeats included. Next you'll collapse repeated values with DISTINCT and count how many different things a column holds.

lessons.title: Count distinct things

lead.text: In the first query of the figure each of the six orders contributes its status, so the word paid appears four times and pending twice. Writing **DISTINCT** straight after `SELECT` removes every row of the result that repeats an *earlier* row, and the second query returns just paid and pending.

afterFigure.text: **The change is made to the result and not to the table**, so the six orders are still stored.

queries.label: The status of every order
queries.sql: SELECT status FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Each status once
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT status FROM orders ORDER BY status;

lead.text: The `amount` column repeats too, since 80 and 20 each occur twice, and it holds one missing value. In the figure the second query keeps one row for 80, one for 20, one for 40, and one for `NULL`, so four rows come back from six.

A missing value is not equal to anything, as the lesson on conditions showed, and yet `DISTINCT` counts all missing values as **the same value** and keeps one row for them. That is **a rule specific to DISTINCT**, and it exists so that the list of values *still shows* that a gap is present.

afterFigure.text: In an ascending sort, SQLite puts that [[NULL|A marker for a value that is missing or unknown, not the same as zero. Met in 'Know what a row represents'.]] row first, because it treats a missing value as smaller than any number. The unknown amount of order 106 is therefore visible in the distinct list, and a reader who sees the `NULL` knows that the column has a gap in it.

queries.label: The amount of every order
queries.sql: SELECT amount FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Each amount once
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT amount FROM orders ORDER BY amount;

queries.label: The customer of every order
queries.sql: SELECT customer_id FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id, id;

queries.label: Each customer once
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id;

lead.text: When `SELECT` lists more than one column, `DISTINCT` treats **two rows as repeats only if every one of those values matches**. The pair (paid, 80) appears twice, in orders 101 and 103, so the second query keeps it once, while (paid, 20) is a different row because its amount differs.
Adding a column to the `SELECT` list can therefore *increase* the number of rows that `DISTINCT` keeps, since more detail makes more rows differ.

afterFigure.text: Taking a column out of the `SELECT` list can only make more rows match, so the result can shrink. **DISTINCT only removes rows that match completely**, on every column that is selected.

queries.label: The status and amount of every order
queries.sql: SELECT status, amount FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Each combination once
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT status, amount FROM orders ORDER BY status, amount;

queries.label: Each item and status
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT item, status FROM orders ORDER BY item, status;

queries.label: Each customer and status
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, status FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id, status;

lead.text: Often the question is the *number* of different values, and not the values themselves. **COUNT** counts the values it is given, and when the argument is `DISTINCT` followed by a column, it counts each different value once.

**COUNT skips missing values**, so a `NULL` in the column is never counted as a value. That makes `COUNT(DISTINCT column)` the number of different values that are actually *known*, which is not the same as the number of rows `DISTINCT` returns when a `NULL` is among them.

afterFigure.text: Counting different values is how you find the number of customers who ordered, or the number of days with activity, without counting any of them twice.

queries.label: Different days
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT day) AS different_days FROM orders;

queries.label: Different statuses
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT status) AS different_statuses FROM orders;

queries.label: Each amount once
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT amount FROM orders ORDER BY amount;

queries.label: How many different known amounts
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT amount) AS known_amounts FROM orders;

lessons.orientation: Use DISTINCT to collapse repeated rows, and tell apart rows, different values and different combinations of values.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: The query `SELECT status FROM orders` returns six rows, and the word paid appears four times among them. If what you want is the list of statuses the shop uses, the answer is two words, paid and pending.
A count of rows says how many orders there are, whereas **a count of different values says how many kinds of thing there are**, and a report that confuses the two can be wrong by a large factor.

intro.promise: By the end you'll use DISTINCT to remove repeats, say how it treats missing values and combinations, and count the different values in a column.

recap.keyIdea: `DISTINCT` keeps one copy of each repeated row, comparing the whole selected row and treating all NULLs as one value.

blocks.text: **DISTINCT** removes repeated rows from a result by comparing every selected column together, so adding a column can *bring back* rows that a single column made repeat. It keeps one row for all the missing values, and it never alters the stored table.

To count different values, write **COUNT(DISTINCT column)**, which counts each known value once and skips every [[NULL|A marker for a value that is missing or unknown, not the same as zero. Met in 'Know what a row represents'.]]. The number of rows a query returns and the number of different things in a column are separate questions, and `DISTINCT` is how you ask the second.

recap.nextHook: DISTINCT counts different values but still treats each one only as a label. Next you'll summarise rows with totals, averages and extremes, and see what a missing value does to each of them.

lessons.title: Choose the right denominator

lead.text: A query that totals, averages or counts uses an **aggregate** function, which reads many rows and returns one value. `COUNT(*)` counts rows, whatever they hold, and `COUNT(column)` counts only the rows where that column has a value, skipping every `NULL`.
The figure shows a survey in which four pupils were asked how many books they read this month, and one left the box empty, so the first query counts four pupils and the second counts three answers.

afterFigure.text: **Each aggregate in SQL ignores the missing values in its column**, so the number of rows that went into a result can be *smaller* than the number of rows in the table.

queries.label: Count every pupil
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS pupils FROM survey;

queries.label: Count the answers
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(books) AS answers FROM survey;

queries.label: Count every order
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders FROM orders;

queries.label: Count the known amounts
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(amount) AS known_amounts FROM orders;

lead.text: **SUM** adds up the known values of a column and **AVG** gives their average, and both skip the NULLs in the same way that `COUNT(column)` does. `AVG` is therefore the sum of the known values divided by the *number of known values*, and not by the number of rows.

The figure restricts both to customer 3, who placed two orders, 105 for 20 and 106 with no amount. The sum is 20, and the average is also 20, because the sum is divided by the single known amount and not by the two orders. The second query shows the counts behind them: two rows, of which one has an amount.

afterFigure.text: Whenever an average looks odd, **the first thing to check is the second count**, because it is the denominator. An average over one known value says very little, even though the query returns a number without complaint.

queries.label: Sum and average of customer 3
queries.sql: SELECT SUM(amount) AS total, AVG(amount) AS mean FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 3;

queries.label: Rows and known amounts
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders, COUNT(amount) AS known FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 3;

lead.text: **MIN** and **MAX** return the smallest and the largest value in a column, and both skip a missing value, because it has no size. This differs from [[ORDER BY|The clause that sorts a result; a missing value sorts first in an ascending list. Met in 'Make the first row meaningful'.]], which placed a `NULL` at the head of an ascending list, because sorting needs somewhere to put every row.
The second query restricts to customer 3, whose only known amount is the smallest and the largest at once.

afterFigure.text: **A WHERE clause is applied before any aggregate**, so each aggregate works on only the rows that remain.

queries.label: All orders
queries.sql: SELECT MIN(amount) AS smallest, MAX(amount) AS largest FROM orders;

queries.label: Customer 3 only
queries.sql: SELECT MIN(amount) AS smallest, MAX(amount) AS largest FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 3;

queries.label: All orders
queries.sql: SELECT MIN(amount) AS minimum, MAX(amount) AS maximum FROM orders;

queries.label: Pending orders only
queries.sql: SELECT MIN(amount) AS minimum, MAX(amount) AS maximum FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending';

lead.text: Sometimes a missing value should count as something. **COALESCE** takes a list of values and returns the first one that is not `NULL`, so `COALESCE(books, 0)` returns the pupil's answer when there is one and 0 when the box was empty. Wrapped inside an aggregate, it turns every blank into a zero before the function sees it.
The first query skips the blank and averages the three answers, and the second counts the blank as a pupil who read nothing, which *lowers* the average.

afterFigure.text: **Neither query is wrong**, because they answer different questions, and `COALESCE` is how you write down which one you mean.

queries.label: Known answers only
queries.sql: SELECT AVG(books) AS mean FROM survey;

queries.label: A blank counted as zero
queries.sql: SELECT AVG(COALESCE(books, 0)) AS mean FROM survey;

queries.label: Skip the missing amount
queries.sql: SELECT SUM(amount) AS total, AVG(amount) AS mean FROM orders;

queries.label: Fill the missing amount with zero
queries.sql: SELECT SUM(COALESCE(amount, 0)) AS total, AVG(COALESCE(amount, 0)) AS mean FROM orders;

lead.text: A `WHERE` clause can remove every row, and an aggregate query then has nothing to read. **It still returns one row**, because an aggregate always produces a single value. `COUNT(*)` reports 0, since there are no rows, while `SUM`, `AVG` and `MAX` report `NULL`, since there is no value to add, to average or to rank.

afterFigure.text: That means **an empty result is visible and not misleading**, because a zero average would *claim* that values existed and cancelled out.

queries.label: All six orders
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders, AVG(amount) AS mean, MAX(amount) AS largest FROM orders;

queries.label: Amounts over 100
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders, AVG(amount) AS mean, MAX(amount) AS largest FROM orders WHERE amount > 100;

queries.label: All orders
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(amount) AS total, AVG(amount) AS mean FROM orders;

queries.label: No matching orders
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(amount) AS total, AVG(amount) AS mean FROM orders WHERE amount > 100;

lessons.orientation: Use COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX on columns that contain missing values, and know which rows each one used.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: The query `SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders` turns six rows into a single number, and every summary function of this kind has to settle what to do with a row whose value is missing.
SQL settles it by skipping those rows, and **that rule quietly decides the denominator**, the number a total is divided by.

intro.promise: By the end you'll use the five basic aggregates, say how many rows each one used, and choose deliberately between skipping a missing value and counting it as zero.

recap.keyIdea: Aggregates skip missing values, so the denominator of an average is the number of known values, and `COALESCE` is how you choose a different treatment.

blocks.text: An **aggregate** reads many rows and returns one value. `COUNT(*)` counts rows, while `COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN` and `MAX` applied to a column skip its NULLs, so an average is the sum of the known values divided by how many there were.

Wrapping a column in **COALESCE(column, 0)** turns each blank into a zero first, which changes the question the average answers. Over no rows at all, `COUNT(*)` gives 0 and the other aggregates give `NULL`, so a missing result means that there was *nothing* to summarise.

recap.nextHook: Each query so far has summarised the whole table into one row. Next you'll split the rows into groups and produce one summary row for each group.

lessons.title: Build a grouped report

lead.text: Adding **GROUP BY status** to a query sorts the rows into groups of orders that share the same status and returns one result row for each group. The [[aggregates|A function that reads many rows and returns one value. Met in 'Choose the right denominator'.]] in the `SELECT` list are then worked out inside every group separately.
In the figure the first query counts the orders in each group, which gives 4 paid and 2 pending, and the second adds up their amounts.

afterFigure.text: **Each result row stands for a group and not for an order**. The totals of 200 and 40 add up to 240, which is what a single `SUM` over the whole table would give, and that agreement is a quick check that no order has been lost or counted *twice*.

queries.label: Orders in each status
queries.sql: SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS orders FROM orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

queries.label: Total of each status
queries.sql: SELECT status, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

lead.text: The column after `GROUP BY` is the answer to the question of **what a row in the report stands for**, now asked of a result and not of a stored table.

The figure groups the orders by day. The counts are 1, 2, 2 and 1, one for each of four days, and the totals follow the same days. On the last day the only order is number 106, whose amount is missing, so the group has no known amount to add up and its total is `NULL` and *not* 0.

afterFigure.text: Group sizes and group totals together tell you how much of a result is built on real values.

queries.label: Orders on each day
queries.sql: SELECT day, COUNT(*) AS orders FROM orders GROUP BY day ORDER BY day;

queries.label: Total for each day
queries.sql: SELECT day, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY day ORDER BY day;

queries.label: Group by item
queries.sql: SELECT item, COUNT(*) AS orders FROM orders GROUP BY item ORDER BY item;

queries.label: Group by status
queries.sql: SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS orders FROM orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

lead.text: The distinction from the last lesson carries into every group. `COUNT(*)` gives the number of rows in the group and [[COUNT(amount)|Counts only the rows where amount has a value. Met in 'Choose the right denominator'.]] gives the number of those rows that have an amount, and the two can differ within one group while agreeing in another.
All four paid orders have an amount, so the two counts agree, whereas of the two pending orders only one has an amount, and the pending total of 40 is therefore built from a single known amount.

afterFigure.text: **Reading the counts beside a total is how you see what the total rests on.**

queries.label: Counts in each status
queries.sql: SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS orders, COUNT(amount) AS known_amounts FROM orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

queries.label: Counts and a total
queries.sql: SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS orders, COUNT(amount) AS known_amounts, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

queries.label: Order counts
queries.sql: SELECT item, COUNT(*) AS orders FROM orders GROUP BY item ORDER BY item;

queries.label: Order counts and known amounts
queries.sql: SELECT item, COUNT(*) AS orders, COUNT(amount) AS known_amounts FROM orders GROUP BY item ORDER BY item;

lead.text: **A WHERE clause in a grouped query is applied first**, to the individual rows, and only the rows that pass are sorted into groups. A group's figures are therefore built from the rows that survived the filter, and a row that was removed can *no longer* contribute to any total.

The figure totals the orders by customer. The first query uses every order and the second only the paid ones. Customers 1 and 3 have the same total in both, because customer 1's orders are all paid and customer 3's pending order has no amount to lose, while customer 2 drops from 120 to 80, because the pending lamp of 40 was removed before the amounts were added.

afterFigure.text: It helps to read a grouped query in the order the database performs it: filter the rows with `WHERE`, group what is left, then calculate the figures for each group. The `WHERE` clause belongs to the *rows*, and not to the groups that come later.

queries.label: Every order
queries.sql: SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY customer_id;

queries.label: Paid orders only
queries.sql: SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY customer_id;

lead.text: Sometimes the condition is about a group and not about a row, such as customers whose total is at least 100. A total does not exist until the groups have been formed, so `WHERE` cannot test it, because `WHERE` runs *before* any group exists. The clause for this is **HAVING**, which is applied to each finished group and keeps only the groups for which its condition is true.

The first query in the figure keeps customers 1 and 2, whose totals are at least 100. The second does both jobs at once: `WHERE` keeps the paid rows, the rows are grouped, and `HAVING` then tests the paid totals, so that only customer 1 remains.

afterFigure.text: The three clauses therefore form a sequence, with `WHERE` choosing rows, `GROUP BY` forming groups and `HAVING` choosing groups. **A condition on an ordinary column belongs in WHERE, and a condition on SUM, COUNT or AVG belongs in HAVING.**

queries.label: Customer totals of at least 100
queries.sql: SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id HAVING SUM(amount) >= 100 ORDER BY customer_id;

queries.label: Paid totals of at least 100
queries.sql: SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' GROUP BY customer_id HAVING SUM(amount) >= 100 ORDER BY customer_id;

queries.label: Status totals of at least 100
queries.sql: SELECT status, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY status HAVING SUM(amount) >= 100 ORDER BY status;

queries.label: Status totals of at least 300
queries.sql: SELECT status, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY status HAVING SUM(amount) >= 300 ORDER BY status;

queries.label: Totals of every item
queries.sql: SELECT item, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY item ORDER BY item;

queries.label: Paid totals of at least 50
queries.sql: SELECT item, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' GROUP BY item HAVING SUM(amount) >= 50 ORDER BY item;

lessons.orientation: Group rows with GROUP BY to produce one summary row per group, then use WHERE for rows and HAVING for groups.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: The query `SELECT SUM(amount) FROM orders` returns one total for the whole table, whereas a report usually needs **one total for each of something**: each status, each customer, each day.
That changes what a row of the result stands for, and once the result has groups in it there are two different places to filter, *before* the groups are formed and *after* their totals are known.

intro.promise: By the end you'll build a report with one row for each group, count and total inside each group, and put each condition in WHERE or HAVING according to what it tests.

recap.keyIdea: `GROUP BY` returns one row for each group, `WHERE` filters the rows before grouping, and `HAVING` filters the groups after their totals are known.

blocks.text: **GROUP BY** sorts the rows into groups that share a value and returns one row for each, so the grouping column tells you what a row of the report stands for. Inside a group, `COUNT(*)` counts the orders, `COUNT(column)` counts the known values, and `SUM` skips the missing amounts.

**WHERE** removes rows before grouping and changes every total, and **HAVING** removes whole groups once their totals exist. Reading a grouped query in that sequence, filter rows, group, calculate, filter groups, shows *exactly* what it returns.

recap.nextHook: Every query so far has read one table. Next you'll follow a stored reference from one table to another and join the matching rows.

lessons.title: Follow a relationship between tables

lead.text: A **JOIN** combines the rows of two tables. The condition written after the word **ON** says when a row of one table matches a row of the other, and `c.id = o.customer_id` is true when the customer's id equals the customer id held in the order. The letters `c` and `o` are short names for the two tables, given with `AS`.

An **INNER JOIN**, which is what `JOIN` means when it stands alone, keeps *only* the pairs of rows for which the condition is true, and each pair becomes one row of the result with columns taken from both tables.

afterFigure.text: Order 101 holds the customer id 1, which is Ada's id, so the pair is kept and Ada's name appears beside the order. A join puts facts stored in separate tables back together whenever a question needs them.

queries.label: Order 101
queries.sql: SELECT o.id AS order_id, c.name AS customer FROM orders AS o JOIN customers AS c ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.id = 101;

queries.label: Order 104
queries.sql: SELECT o.id AS order_id, c.name AS customer FROM orders AS o JOIN customers AS c ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.id = 104;

lead.text: The figure joins a table of pupils to a table of clubs. Each pupil holds the id of one club, and the condition `p.club = c.id` matches the pupil with that club. The first query starts from the pupils and the second starts from the clubs, and both return the same four pairs, because **a join is symmetrical in what it matches** and the order of the tables changes only the order of the columns and rows.

The result has a row for every *pair* that matched and not a row for every pupil or for every club. When two pupils belong to the same club, that club's name therefore appears twice, once in each pair.

afterFigure.text: So **the number of rows in a join is the number of matching pairs**. It can be larger than either table, when one row matches many, and it can be smaller, when some rows match nothing.

queries.label: Pupils with their club
queries.sql: SELECT p.name AS pupil, c.name AS club FROM pupils AS p JOIN clubs AS c ON c.id = p.club ORDER BY p.id;

queries.label: Clubs with their pupils
queries.sql: SELECT c.name AS club, p.name AS pupil FROM clubs AS c JOIN pupils AS p ON p.club = c.id ORDER BY c.id, p.id;

queries.label: The reference in each order
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Each order with its customer's name
queries.sql: SELECT o.id, c.name, o.amount FROM orders AS o JOIN customers AS c ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id;

lead.text: In the first query of the figure the customer's name is repeated, because the join produces **one row for every order** and each customer placed two.

When the question is about customers rather than orders, [[DISTINCT|Removes repeated rows from a result, comparing the whole selected row. Met in 'Count distinct things'.]] removes the repeats, as the second query does.

queries.label: One row for each order
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id;

queries.label: Each customer who ordered, once
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT c.name FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY c.name;

lead.text: A join without a matching condition pairs everything with everything, and SQL has a name for it, **CROSS JOIN**. Every row of the first table is combined with every row of the second, so a table of 2 rows crossed with a table of 3 rows gives 2 times 3, or 6, rows.

A cross join is the right tool when every combination is wanted, as in a menu of meal deals, and the *wrong* one whenever a stored reference links the rows, because it then pairs rows that have nothing to do with each other.

afterFigure.text: Two tables of a thousand rows would produce a million. **The ON condition is what cuts a join down from the product to the pairs that mean something.**

queries.label: Every combination
queries.sql: SELECT m.item AS main, d.drink FROM mains AS m CROSS JOIN drinks AS d ORDER BY m.item, d.drink;

queries.label: How many combinations
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS combinations FROM mains CROSS JOIN drinks;

queries.label: Pairs that match the reference
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY c.id, o.id;

queries.label: Every possible pair
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c CROSS JOIN orders AS o ORDER BY c.id, o.id;

lead.text: A join runs without complaint on any condition that can be evaluated, and that includes conditions that do not mean what you intended. In the figure the first query follows the club number stored in each pupil, `p.club = c.id`, and pairs every pupil with their own club.

The second query compares the pupil's own id with the club's id instead. Pupil 3 is then paired with club 3 and pupil 4 with club 4, so Cy appears with Drama and Di with Art, and the result still looks like a tidy list of pupils and clubs. Only the first two rows come out right, and they do so by *coincidence*.

afterFigure.text: **Nothing in the output warns you of a wrong condition**, so the check has to be made against the data. Ask which column was designed to refer to the other table, and join on that column and on the [[primary key|A column whose values never repeat, so each value picks out one row. Met in 'Know what a row represents'.]] it refers to.

queries.label: Following the club number
queries.sql: SELECT p.name AS pupil, c.name AS club FROM pupils AS p JOIN clubs AS c ON c.id = p.club ORDER BY p.id;

queries.label: Comparing the ids
queries.sql: SELECT p.name AS pupil, c.name AS club FROM pupils AS p JOIN clubs AS c ON c.id = p.id ORDER BY p.id;

lessons.orientation: Use a join to put matching rows of two tables side by side, and say exactly how many pairs a join condition produces.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: The `orders` table records that order 104 belongs to customer 2, but it holds *no* name, because the name is stored once in the `customers` table next to the id 2. A report that lists each order with the name of the customer who placed it therefore **needs both tables at once**.
A join does that by following the reference: for each order it finds the customer whose id the order holds and places the two rows side by side.

intro.promise: By the end you'll write the condition that links two tables, count the rows an inner join returns, and say what a cross join does and why it is rarely wanted.

recap.keyIdea: An inner join returns one row for each pair of rows that satisfies its ON condition, and a cross join returns every pair.

blocks.text: A **JOIN** pairs the rows of two tables whose columns satisfy the **ON condition**, and the sensible condition follows the stored reference, such as `c.id = o.customer_id`. An inner join returns one row for each matching pair, so a customer with several orders appears *several* times and a customer with none does not appear.

A **CROSS JOIN** has no condition and returns every pairing, the product of the two table sizes. A condition that runs but compares the wrong columns still returns a tidy result, so the condition has to be checked against what the columns mean.

recap.nextHook: An inner join drops the customers who have no orders, which is exactly what a report on customers must not do. Next you'll keep every customer and show the gaps.

lessons.title: Keep the customers with no orders

lead.text: An [[inner join|Keeps only the pairs of rows that satisfy the ON condition. Met in 'Follow a relationship between tables'.]] pairs only the rows that match, so a customer with no orders vanishes from its result. A **LEFT JOIN** keeps every row of the table on its left, the one named before the words `LEFT JOIN`, and pairs it with the matching rows of the right-hand table when there are any. **A left row that finds no match still appears, once,** with `NULL` in every column that would have come from the right-hand table.
Ada has two orders, so she appears in two pairs. Dee has none, so she appears in a single row whose order column is `NULL`.

afterFigure.text: That `NULL` does *not* mean that a stored order has lost its id. It marks the absence of a match, since there is no order to show beside Dee.

queries.label: A customer with orders
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE c.id = 1 ORDER BY o.id;

queries.label: A customer with none
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE c.id = 4 ORDER BY o.id;

lead.text: The figure joins clubs to pupils, with the clubs on the left. The `LEFT JOIN` returns the four rows of the inner join and one more, for the Art club, which has no pupils: its `pupil` and `year` columns are `NULL` because nothing matched.
**The result now has a row for everything the left table holds.**

afterFigure.text: Not every `NULL` in the result means a *missing match*. The pupil Di belongs to a club, but her year is stored as `NULL` in the `pupils` table, and that `NULL` appears in the inner join as well. **A NULL in a column from the right-hand table can come from either source**, which matters in the next steps.

queries.label: Matches only
queries.sql: SELECT c.name AS club, p.name AS pupil, p.year FROM clubs AS c JOIN pupils AS p ON p.club = c.id ORDER BY c.id, p.id;

queries.label: Every club kept
queries.sql: SELECT c.name AS club, p.name AS pupil, p.year FROM clubs AS c LEFT JOIN pupils AS p ON p.club = c.id ORDER BY c.id, p.id;

queries.label: Matches only
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id, o.amount FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY c.id, o.id;

queries.label: Every customer kept
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id, o.amount FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY c.id, o.id;

lead.text: A `LEFT JOIN` followed by a count raises a trap. The unmatched left row is a *real* row of the join result, so `COUNT(*)` counts it, and a club with no pupils is reported as having one. **COUNT of a column from the right-hand table skips NULL**, and for an unmatched row every such column is `NULL`, so it counts only the rows that really matched.

In the figure the first query counts rows and reports one pupil for the Art club, which has none. The second counts the pupil ids, and it reports 0 for the same club, together with the right counts for the other three.

afterFigure.text: **The safest column to count is the key of the right-hand table**, because every stored row in these tables has its key, so the key is missing only when there was no match. A count over the joined rows answers how many rows the join produced, whereas a count of that key answers how many things were matched.

queries.label: Counting the rows
queries.sql: SELECT c.name AS club, COUNT(*) AS joined_rows FROM clubs AS c LEFT JOIN pupils AS p ON p.club = c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.name ORDER BY c.id;

queries.label: Counting the pupil ids
queries.sql: SELECT c.name AS club, COUNT(p.id) AS pupils FROM clubs AS c LEFT JOIN pupils AS p ON p.club = c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.name ORDER BY c.id;

queries.label: Counting the rows
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, COUNT(*) AS rows FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id GROUP BY c.id, c.name ORDER BY c.id;

queries.label: Counting the order ids
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS orders FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id GROUP BY c.id, c.name ORDER BY c.id;

lead.text: Suppose only the pupils in year 6 should be matched with their clubs. Written in the `WHERE` clause, the test `p.year = 6` is applied after the join, to every row, and a row whose pupil columns are `NULL` cannot satisfy it, so the clubs that matched no year-6 pupil are discarded and the `LEFT JOIN` behaves like an inner join.

Written in the `ON` condition, the same test narrows what counts as a match and *nothing more*. The second query in the figure has it in `WHERE` and returns two rows. The first has it in `ON`, and it keeps all four clubs, with the pupil shown only where a year-6 pupil exists, so that Drama and Art appear with `NULL`.

afterFigure.text: **The rule is to put a condition on the right-hand table in ON when every left row must survive**, and in `WHERE` only when you really do want to discard the left rows that did not match.

queries.label: The test in ON
queries.sql: SELECT c.name AS club, p.name AS pupil FROM clubs AS c LEFT JOIN pupils AS p ON p.club = c.id AND p.year = 6 ORDER BY c.id, p.id;

queries.label: The test in WHERE
queries.sql: SELECT c.name AS club, p.name AS pupil FROM clubs AS c LEFT JOIN pupils AS p ON p.club = c.id WHERE p.year = 6 ORDER BY c.id, p.id;

lead.text: A `LEFT JOIN` also answers the opposite question: which left rows have no match at all? Keep the join, then ask `WHERE` to keep only the rows where the right-hand key `IS NULL`. **Since every stored row in these tables has its key, a NULL there can only mean that no row matched.**
The second query tests the pupil's year instead and returns Drama as well, with Di beside it, although Di is a *perfectly good* match: her year is a stored `NULL`.

afterFigure.text: The choice of column is therefore part of the logic. **Test a column that cannot be NULL when it is stored**, normally the key, and the `NULL` will always mean what you intend it to mean. SQLite guarantees this for an `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY`, whereas a key of any other type, such as a text name, can hold a `NULL` unless the column is also declared `NOT NULL`.

queries.label: Testing the pupil's id
queries.sql: SELECT c.name AS club, p.name AS pupil FROM clubs AS c LEFT JOIN pupils AS p ON p.club = c.id WHERE p.id IS NULL ORDER BY c.id;

queries.label: Testing the pupil's year
queries.sql: SELECT c.name AS club, p.name AS pupil FROM clubs AS c LEFT JOIN pupils AS p ON p.club = c.id WHERE p.year IS NULL ORDER BY c.id, p.id;

lessons.orientation: Use a LEFT JOIN to keep every row of the left table, read the NULLs it creates, and put each test and count where it belongs.
lessons.reviewLabel: Keep the customers with no orders
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: An inner join answers questions about orders well, but it has no way to answer which customers have not ordered anything, because a customer without an order matches nothing and is **dropped without a trace**. Dee, who has no orders at all, is exactly the row that this question is about.

Keeping her takes a different join, one in which every customer stays and the columns that would have come from an order are left empty. Those empty cells are NULLs, and a `NULL` of this kind records a match that was *never found*, which is a different fact from a value *missing from a stored table*.

intro.promise: By the end you'll keep every row of the left table in a join, count matches without counting blanks, and place a condition in ON or WHERE according to what it should do.

recap.keyIdea: A `LEFT JOIN` keeps every left row and fills the right-hand columns with `NULL` where nothing matched, so counts and tests must be written to tell a blank match from a stored value.

blocks.text: A **LEFT JOIN** keeps every row of the left table, pairing it with its matches and showing `NULL` in the right-hand columns when there are none. To count matches, count a key from the right-hand table, since `COUNT(*)` counts the blank row as well.

A condition on the right-hand table belongs in **ON** when every left row must survive, because `WHERE` discards the blank rows. To find the left rows with no match, test the right-hand key with **IS NULL**, because every stored row has its key.

recap.nextHook: A LEFT JOIN protects the rows on one side only. Next you'll see what happens to an order that has no customer, and how to keep unmatched rows on both sides.

lessons.title: Keep unmatched rows on either side

lead.text: One small table lists the guests who replied, Ana, Ben and Cy, and the other lists the badges that were printed, for Ben, Cy and Dot. Ana replied but has no badge, and Dot has a badge but never replied.

A [[LEFT JOIN|Keeps every row of the left table, with NULL where nothing matched. Met in 'Keep the customers with no orders'.]] from the guests keeps every guest, so Ana appears with a `NULL` badge, and Dot is left out. A **RIGHT JOIN** keeps every row of the table on its right instead, so the badges are all kept, Dot appears with a `NULL` guest, and Ana is left out. It is a `LEFT JOIN` with the roles of the two tables exchanged.

afterFigure.text: **Each join protects one side**, depending on which table is written first. SQLite supported only `LEFT JOIN` until version 3.39.0, released in 2022, which is *why* older tutorials say that it has no `RIGHT JOIN`.

queries.label: Every guest kept
queries.sql: SELECT g.name AS guest, b.name AS badge FROM guests AS g LEFT JOIN badges AS b ON b.name = g.name ORDER BY g.name;

queries.label: Every badge kept
queries.sql: SELECT g.name AS guest, b.name AS badge FROM guests AS g RIGHT JOIN badges AS b ON b.name = g.name ORDER BY b.name;

lead.text: When neither kind of leftover may be lost, you need the join that protects both sides, the **FULL OUTER JOIN**. It returns every matching pair, then every unmatched row of the left table with NULLs on the right, then every unmatched row of the right table with NULLs on the left.

The full join adds Ana, whose `badge` column is `NULL`, and Dot, whose `guest` column is `NULL`, and the `ORDER BY` uses [[COALESCE|Returns the first value that is not NULL. Met in 'Choose the right denominator'.]] so that the rows sort by whichever name exists.

afterFigure.text: Each row of a full join is therefore one of three kinds: **a pair, a left row with nothing to match, or a right row with nothing to match**.

queries.label: Matches only
queries.sql: SELECT g.name AS guest, b.name AS badge FROM guests AS g INNER JOIN badges AS b ON b.name = g.name ORDER BY g.name;

queries.label: Both sides kept
queries.sql: SELECT g.name AS guest, b.name AS badge FROM guests AS g FULL OUTER JOIN badges AS b ON b.name = g.name ORDER BY COALESCE(g.name, b.name);

queries.label: Customers preserved
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id, c.id;

queries.label: Orders preserved
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c RIGHT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id, c.id;

queries.label: Matches only
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c INNER JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id, c.id;

queries.label: Both sides kept
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c FULL OUTER JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id, c.id;

lead.text: The figure counts the rows of three joins over the shop's tables, and two of the counts agree. The `LEFT JOIN` and the `RIGHT JOIN` both return seven rows, yet **they are not the same seven**: the first holds Dee, a customer with no order, and the second holds order 107, an order with no customer.
The full join returns eight, which is the six matched pairs together with both leftovers. Its count exceeds the others by exactly one because each of them lacks one of the two.

afterFigure.text: A row count is a useful check but it cannot tell you *which* records were kept. When two joins are being compared, **look at which unmatched rows each one preserves**, and not only at how many rows come back.

queries.label: LEFT JOIN rows
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id;

queries.label: RIGHT JOIN rows
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows FROM customers AS c RIGHT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id;

queries.label: FULL OUTER JOIN rows
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows FROM customers AS c FULL OUTER JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id;

lead.text: In the guests and badges example, **a NULL in the badge column marks a guest with no badge**, and a `NULL` in the `guest` column marks a badge with no guest, and each case can be isolated by testing the key on the side that is missing.
A pair, in which both names are present, passes neither test.

afterFigure.text: The column to test must be one that is never `NULL` in a stored row, usually the key, or a missing *partner* is confused with a missing *value*.

queries.label: The badge is NULL
queries.sql: SELECT g.name AS guest, b.name AS badge FROM guests AS g FULL OUTER JOIN badges AS b ON b.name = g.name WHERE b.name IS NULL ORDER BY g.name;

queries.label: The guest is NULL
queries.sql: SELECT g.name AS guest, b.name AS badge FROM guests AS g FULL OUTER JOIN badges AS b ON b.name = g.name WHERE g.name IS NULL ORDER BY b.name;

queries.label: First test
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c FULL OUTER JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.id IS NULL ORDER BY c.id;

queries.label: Second test
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c FULL OUTER JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE c.id IS NULL ORDER BY o.id;

steps.headline: A test in the ON condition

lead.text: A condition in ON decides what counts as a match, and **a full join keeps whatever fails to match from either side**. In the figure the second query adds `b.colour = 'blue'` to the matching condition. Cy's badge is red, so the pair no longer matches, and Cy appears twice: once as a guest with a `NULL` badge and once as a badge with a `NULL` guest.

*Nothing* has been discarded, since the person and the badge are both still in the result. They have simply stopped being a pair. **That is the difference from a test in WHERE, which would remove rows from the result.**

afterFigure.text: Whenever a full join has an extra test in ON, expect that some earlier pairs will have fallen apart into two unmatched rows, so the result can grow.

queries.label: Match on name
queries.sql: SELECT g.name AS guest, b.name AS badge FROM guests AS g FULL OUTER JOIN badges AS b ON b.name = g.name ORDER BY COALESCE(g.name, b.name);

queries.label: Match on name and a blue badge
queries.sql: SELECT g.name AS guest, b.name AS badge FROM guests AS g FULL OUTER JOIN badges AS b ON b.name = g.name AND b.colour = 'blue' ORDER BY COALESCE(g.name, b.name), b.name;

queries.label: Any order can match
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id, o.status FROM customers AS c FULL OUTER JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE c.id IS NULL ORDER BY o.id;

queries.label: Only paid orders can match
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id, o.status FROM customers AS c FULL OUTER JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id AND o.status = 'paid' WHERE c.id IS NULL ORDER BY o.id;

lessons.orientation: Use RIGHT and FULL OUTER joins to keep unmatched rows from either side, and read the NULLs they create.
lessons.reviewLabel: Keep unmatched rows on either side
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: The shop has taken a guest order: order 107, a mug for 30, placed by someone who is not a customer, so its `customer_id` is `NULL`. The join that keeps all customers keeps Dee but still leaves order 107 out.

A complete reconciliation of customers and orders has to account for both kinds of exception, **the customer with no order and the order with no customer**, since a report that keeps only one of them loses the other without any warning.

intro.promise: By the end you'll choose between LEFT, RIGHT, FULL and inner joins, count the rows each returns, and read the NULLs on either side of a full join.

recap.keyIdea: A `RIGHT JOIN` keeps the unmatched rows of the right table and a `FULL OUTER JOIN` keeps those of both tables, with NULLs marking the side that had no partner.

blocks.text: A **RIGHT JOIN** preserves the table on its right, a `LEFT JOIN` preserves the table on its left, and a **FULL OUTER JOIN** preserves both, so each row of a full join is a pair, a left row with no partner or a right row with no partner. The NULLs show which kind of row you are reading, and a key is the right column to test.

A test placed in [[ON|The condition that says when a row of one table matches a row of the other. Met in 'Follow a relationship between tables'.]] decides what counts as a match, so a full join keeps both rows of a pair that fails it. Two joins can return the same number of rows and still keep different unmatched records, so compare which side each preserves and *not only* the count.

recap.nextHook: Joins bring columns from two tables into one row. Next you'll use one query to define a value or a list for another, without multiplying its rows.

lessons.title: Use one query to define another

lead.text: A **subquery** is a `SELECT` written in brackets inside another query. When it returns a single value, as `AVG(amount)` does, it can be used wherever a value is wanted, including on the right of a comparison. **The database runs the inner query first** and the result takes the place of the whole bracket, so that `WHERE amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders)` behaves as if the average had been typed in.

The first query in the figure returns the [[average|The sum of the known values divided by how many there are. Met in 'Choose the right denominator'.]] of the orders' amounts: a total of 240 over the 5 orders that have an amount, which is why the average is 48 and not 40.

afterFigure.text: If the orders change, the subquery is run again and the comparison follows, which a typed-in number would *not* do.

queries.label: The average on its own
queries.sql: SELECT AVG(amount) AS average FROM orders;

queries.label: What the average is built from
queries.sql: SELECT SUM(amount) AS total, COUNT(amount) AS known_amounts FROM orders;

queries.label: Above the average
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders) ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Above a fixed 80
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount > 80 ORDER BY id;

lead.text: A subquery can also return several rows of one column, and then **it plays the part of a list**. The condition `customer_id IN (SELECT id FROM customers WHERE region = 'North')` keeps the orders whose customer id appears in the list that the inner query produces, so the inner query decides who counts as North and the outer query reads the orders.

The figure shows the lists themselves. The North list holds customers 1 and 3, Ada and Cy, and the South list holds customer 2, Ben. Substituting a list into [[IN|True when a value equals any value in a list. Met in 'Write the condition you mean'.]] is the same as writing the ids out, except that the list is rebuilt from the `customers` table *every time* the query runs.

afterFigure.text: A join to `customers` would answer the same question here, but **a subquery cannot multiply the rows of the outer query**, because it never adds columns or pairs to the outer query's rows.

queries.label: The North list
queries.sql: SELECT id, name FROM customers WHERE region = 'North' ORDER BY id;

queries.label: The South list
queries.sql: SELECT id, name FROM customers WHERE region = 'South' ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Orders of North customers
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, amount FROM orders WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT id FROM customers WHERE region = 'North') ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Orders of South customers
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, amount FROM orders WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT id FROM customers WHERE region = 'South') ORDER BY id;

lead.text: **EXISTS** followed by a subquery is true when that subquery returns at least one row and false when it returns none, and `NOT EXISTS` reverses it. In the figure the inner query asks, for each customer in turn, whether any order has a `customer_id` equal to `c.id`.

The first query keeps Ada, Ben and Cy, and the second finds Dee, which is the question the [[LEFT JOIN|Keeps every row of the left table, with NULL where nothing matched. Met in 'Keep the customers with no orders'.]] answered in an earlier lesson, now asked directly.

afterFigure.text: **EXISTS gives only a yes or a no**, and it does not matter what the inner query selects, which is why `SELECT 1` is the usual choice.

queries.label: Customers with an order
queries.sql: SELECT c.id, c.name FROM customers AS c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders AS o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) ORDER BY c.id;

queries.label: Customers with no order
queries.sql: SELECT c.id, c.name FROM customers AS c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders AS o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) ORDER BY c.id;

lead.text: The inner query in an [[EXISTS|True when the subquery returns at least one row. Met earlier in 'Use one query to define another'.]] test mentions `c.id`, a column of the outer query, so its result depends on which outer row is being examined. A subquery that does this is called **correlated**. In effect it is run once for each outer row, with that row's value substituted in.

The first query in the figure gives each customer's average order, which is 50, 60 and 20. The second keeps the orders that exceed the average of *their own customer's* orders: order 101, at 80 against Ada's 50, and order 103, at 80 against Ben's 60. Order 105 equals Cy's average of 20 and does not exceed it.

afterFigure.text: A subquery with no reference to the outer row, like the overall average, has the same answer throughout and is run once. **A correlated one is how a row is compared with its own group** without collapsing the groups into single rows.

queries.label: Each customer's average
queries.sql: SELECT customer_id, AVG(amount) AS average FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY customer_id;

queries.label: Orders above their customer's average
queries.sql: SELECT o.id, o.customer_id, o.amount FROM orders AS o WHERE o.amount > (SELECT AVG(i.amount) FROM orders AS i WHERE i.customer_id = o.customer_id) ORDER BY o.id;

queries.label: Above the overall average
queries.sql: SELECT id, item, amount FROM orders WHERE amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders) ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Above the average for its own item
queries.sql: SELECT o.id, o.item, o.amount FROM orders AS o WHERE o.amount > (SELECT AVG(i.amount) FROM orders AS i WHERE i.item = o.item) ORDER BY o.id;

lessons.orientation: Use a query inside another query to supply a value, a list or a yes-or-no test, without multiplying the outer rows.
lessons.reviewLabel: Use one query to define another
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: Which orders are larger than the average order? The sentence sounds like one question, but **it contains two**: what is the average, and which orders exceed it? `WHERE amount > AVG(amount)` is not allowed, because `WHERE` looks at one row at a time and an average needs *all* of them.
The way out is to let one query answer the first question and hand its result to the other.

intro.promise: By the end you'll use a subquery as a value, as a list for IN and as an EXISTS test, and say when a subquery depends on the row of the outer query.

recap.keyIdea: A subquery supplies a value, a list or an existence test to an outer query, and it never multiplies the outer query's rows.

blocks.text: A **subquery** is a `SELECT` inside brackets. A scalar one returns a single value, such as the average, to compare with; one that returns a column can follow `IN` as a list; and **EXISTS** asks only whether the inner query finds a row.

A **correlated** subquery refers to the outer row and is worked out again for each one, which lets a row be compared with its own group. Because the outer query supplies the rows, none of these devices can *repeat* them, unlike a join that matches several rows.
