recap.nextHook: A subquery builds one result from another. Next you'll stack two results on top of each other with UNION and decide whether repeated rows stay.

lessons.title: Combine reports deliberately

lead.text: **UNION** joins two `SELECT` statements into one result by putting the rows of the second under the rows of the first. The two must return the same number of columns, because they are stacked, and **the columns are matched by position and not by name**. The first `SELECT` supplies the headings of the result.

afterFigure.text: `UNION` differs from a [[join|Pairs the rows of two tables whose columns satisfy the ON condition. Met in 'Follow a relationship between tables'.]] in *direction*. A join places rows side by side and adds columns; a union stacks rows and keeps the columns as they are.

queries.label: Chess club
queries.sql: SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'chess' ORDER BY name;

queries.label: Drama club
queries.sql: SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'drama' ORDER BY name;

lead.text: Plain `UNION` treats the stacked rows as a set, in the way that [[DISTINCT|Removes repeated rows from a result. Met in 'Count distinct things'.]] does: **a row that appears in both results is kept once**. In the first query of the figure, Cy and Di, who belong to both clubs, appear one time each and the list has six names.

**UNION ALL** stacks the rows and removes *nothing*, so the second query returns eight rows, with Cy and Di twice each. A list of people should name each person once, whereas a total over the combined rows should count every row, including the repeats.

afterFigure.text: `UNION ALL` is also faster, because the database does not have to compare the rows to find repeats.

queries.label: UNION, repeats removed
queries.sql: SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'chess' UNION SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'drama' ORDER BY name;

queries.label: UNION ALL, every row kept
queries.sql: SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'chess' UNION ALL SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'drama' ORDER BY name;

queries.label: Paid orders
queries.sql: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Orders of at least 40
queries.sql: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

lead.text: **A repeat means a row that matches another in every column.** The first query in the figure stacks the names alone, so Cy from the chess list and Cy from the drama list are the same row, and only one is kept.

The second query adds a column that states the club, written as `'chess' AS club` in one `SELECT` and `'drama' AS club` in the other. Cy now appears as (Cy, chess) and (Cy, drama), which are *different* rows, so both survive and the result has eight rows. A fixed text value in a `SELECT` list gives every row of that query the same value in a new column, and it is the usual way to record which result a row came from.

afterFigure.text: The label turns `UNION` from a list of distinct people into a list of memberships. **Adding or removing a column is therefore a decision about what counts as the same row**, and it should be taken deliberately.

queries.label: Names only
queries.sql: SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'chess' UNION SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'drama' ORDER BY name;

queries.label: Names with the club
queries.sql: SELECT name, 'chess' AS club FROM members WHERE club = 'chess' UNION SELECT name, 'drama' AS club FROM members WHERE club = 'drama' ORDER BY name, club;

queries.label: Paid orders, labelled
queries.sql: SELECT id, 'paid' AS selection FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Large orders, labelled
queries.sql: SELECT id, 'large' AS selection FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

lead.text: In a union, `ORDER BY` is written **once, after the last SELECT**, and it sorts the whole combined result by the headings of the first `SELECT`, because the order of the parts is lost when they are stacked.

[[LIMIT|Keeps the first rows of an ordered result. Met in 'Make the first row meaningful'.]] follows in the same way. The limit is applied after the stacking, the removal of repeats and the sorting, so it cuts the *finished* list.

afterFigure.text: The sequence is therefore: run each `SELECT`, stack the rows, remove repeats if the operator is `UNION`, sort, and then limit. Reading a combined query in that order shows exactly which rows it returns.

queries.label: The whole list, sorted
queries.sql: SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'chess' UNION SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'drama' ORDER BY name;

queries.label: The first three names
queries.sql: SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'chess' UNION SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'drama' ORDER BY name LIMIT 3;

queries.label: The combined, sorted result
queries.sql: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' UNION SELECT id FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: The first three ids
queries.sql: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' UNION SELECT id FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id LIMIT 3;

lessons.orientation: Use UNION and UNION ALL to stack results into one, decide whether repeated rows stay, and sort and limit the stacked result.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: The query `SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'chess'` returns Ann, Bo, Cy and Di, and the same query for the drama club returns Cy, Di, Ed and Flo. A list of everyone who belongs to either club needs the rows of both results in one place.

`UNION` does that by putting the rows of the second result under those of the first, so that the two become one. What should then happen to a person who appears in both results is a real decision, because it settles **whether the combined report counts people or counts memberships**.

intro.promise: By the end you'll stack two results with UNION or UNION ALL, say how many rows each returns when the results overlap, and sort the combined list.

recap.keyIdea: `UNION` stacks two results and removes repeated rows, `UNION ALL` keeps every row, and the two results must have matching columns.

blocks.text: **UNION** stacks the rows of one `SELECT` under another, and the two must return the same number of columns, matched by position. It keeps one copy of any row that appears in both, while **UNION ALL** keeps every row, repeats included.
A row counts as a repeat only when every column matches, so a label column can *keep* an overlap. `ORDER BY` and `LIMIT` are written once, at the end, and they apply to the whole stacked result.

recap.nextHook: Stacking combines results without changing any single row. Next you'll rank rows with window functions, which add a calculation beside each row instead of collapsing the rows.

lessons.title: Rank rows without collapsing them

lead.text: A [[grouped query|Returns one row for each group of rows that share a value. Met in 'Build a grouped report'.]] turns many rows into one row for each group. A **window function** works differently: it calculates a value for every row of the result and leaves the rows themselves *in place*.
**ROW_NUMBER()** gives each row the next whole number, and the clause **OVER (ORDER BY id)** says in what order the rows are numbered, so order 101 receives 1, order 102 receives 2, and so on.

afterFigure.text: The word `OVER` marks the difference between a window function and an ordinary aggregate, and what follows it describes the rows that the function may look at.

queries.label: Grouped, one row for each customer
queries.sql: SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS orders FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY customer_id;

queries.label: Windowed, every order kept
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id) AS position FROM orders ORDER BY id;

lead.text: `ROW_NUMBER` always gives each row a different number, even when two rows are equal in the ordering, which is wrong for a leaderboard where tied divers *should* share a place. **RANK()** gives rows that tie the same rank, and **the next rank is the number of rows already placed plus one**.

The figure ranks four divers by points. Eve, Fay and Gus all scored 9. The first query numbers them 1, 2 and 3 only because a tie-breaker, the name, was added, while the second gives all three the rank 1. Hal, with 7 points, then has three divers ahead of him, so his rank is 4, and ranks 2 and 3 are never used.

afterFigure.text: **The gap is deliberate.** It records that three divers finished ahead of Hal, which a rank of 2 would conceal. The gap appears after every tie and is the signature of `RANK`.

queries.label: Every diver numbered
queries.sql: SELECT name, points, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY points DESC, name) AS position FROM divers ORDER BY position;

queries.label: Tied divers share a rank
queries.sql: SELECT name, points, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY points DESC) AS position FROM divers ORDER BY position, name;

queries.label: Every row numbered
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

queries.label: Equal amounts share a rank
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

lead.text: Some reports want the places to run on without gaps: first prize, second prize and third prize, however many people share the first. **DENSE_RANK()** does that. Tied rows share a rank, and the next rank is simply the next whole number, so the ranks count the *different scores* and not the number of rows placed.
They differ on Hal, who has rank 4 under `RANK` and rank 2 under `DENSE_RANK`, because 9 is the first score and 7 is the second.

afterFigure.text: **RANK says how many rows are ahead of this one, whereas DENSE_RANK says how many different values are ahead of it**, and the latter suits categories such as prize bands.

queries.label: RANK, with gaps
queries.sql: SELECT name, points, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY points DESC) AS position FROM divers ORDER BY position, name;

queries.label: DENSE_RANK, without gaps
queries.sql: SELECT name, points, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY points DESC) AS position FROM divers ORDER BY position, name;

queries.label: RANK, with gaps
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

queries.label: DENSE_RANK, without gaps
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

lead.text: **Rows tie when they are equal in every column of the ORDER BY inside OVER.** If you add a second column, the rows are compared on that column whenever the first is equal, and divers who tied on points can then be told apart by their names.
The first query orders by points alone, so the three nines tie and share rank 1. The second orders by points and then by name, and the ties disappear: Eve is 1, Fay is 2, Gus is 3 and Hal is 4.

afterFigure.text: A prize list may want ties to stay, while a list that picks one winner needs a unique order, and a unique column such as the id will always give one.

queries.label: Points only
queries.sql: SELECT name, points, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY points DESC) AS position FROM divers ORDER BY position, name;

queries.label: Points, then name
queries.sql: SELECT name, points, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY points DESC, name) AS position FROM divers ORDER BY position;

queries.label: Rank by amount
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

queries.label: Rank by amount, then id
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

lessons.orientation: Use ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK to put a position beside each row, and choose how ties are treated.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: Ranking the shop's orders by amount looks like a job for `GROUP BY`, but grouping would collapse the orders, and **a ranking needs every order to keep its own row** and to gain a position.

Window functions add a calculated column to every row and leave the rows in place. The question that matters is what two equal rows should receive, because there are three sensible answers and each is a *different function*.

intro.promise: By the end you'll number rows with a window function, and choose between ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK according to how ties should be treated.

recap.keyIdea: `ROW_NUMBER` gives every row its own position, `RANK` gives ties the same position and leaves a gap, and `DENSE_RANK` gives ties the same position without gaps.

blocks.text: A **window function** adds a value beside each row and keeps every row, and the `ORDER BY` inside `OVER` sets the order in which the rows are placed. `ROW_NUMBER` numbers the rows 1, 2, 3 and so on whatever their values, so tied rows *still* receive different numbers.

**RANK** lets tied rows share a position and then skips the positions they used up, while **DENSE_RANK** shares a position and does not skip. Adding a further column inside `OVER` breaks a tie, because rows tie only when they are equal in every ordering column.

recap.nextHook: Every window so far has covered the whole table. Next you'll limit a window to each customer's own rows with PARTITION BY.

lessons.title: Choose which rows a window sees

lead.text: To keep every order and still show its customer's total beside it, a window function needs to know which rows belong together, and **PARTITION BY** tells it. `SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id)` adds up the amounts of the rows that share a customer id and **writes that total on each of those rows**, unlike [[GROUP BY|Sorts the rows into groups and returns one row for each group. Met in 'Build a grouped report'.]].

The first query in the figure returns all six orders, and Ada's two orders each carry the total of 100, which is her 80 and her 20. The second query returns the same totals as a grouped report, with a single row for each customer.

afterFigure.text: The two reports differ in what a *row* stands for: in the grouped one it is a customer, and in the windowed one it is an order, which can therefore be compared with its customer's total.

queries.label: Totals beside the orders
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS customer_total FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Totals as groups
queries.sql: SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS customer_total FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY customer_id;

queries.label: Grouped by status
queries.sql: SELECT status, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

queries.label: Totals beside the orders
queries.sql: SELECT id, status, SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY status) AS total FROM orders ORDER BY id;

lead.text: A window function with no `PARTITION BY` sees all the rows of the result as one window, so a ranking runs straight through them. When `PARTITION BY` is added, **each group is a window of its own**, and a calculation such as [[ROW_NUMBER|Gives each row of a window the next whole number in its ordering. Met in 'Rank rows without collapsing them'.]] begins again at 1 in every group.

The figure numbers three pupils by score. In the first query the pupils of both classes share one window and are numbered 1, 2 and 3. In the second query, `PARTITION BY class` gives each class a window, so Bo and Ann are numbered 1 and 2 within class A, and Cy *begins again* at 1 in class B.

afterFigure.text: The `ORDER BY` inside `OVER` still sets the order within each window, and the partition decides which rows are counted together.

queries.label: One window for the whole sheet
queries.sql: SELECT name, class, score, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS position FROM pupils ORDER BY position;

queries.label: A window for each class
queries.sql: SELECT name, class, score, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY class ORDER BY score DESC) AS position FROM pupils ORDER BY class, position;

queries.label: One window for all orders
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id) AS position FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: A window for each customer
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY id) AS position FROM orders ORDER BY id;

lead.text: Sometimes the aim is not a rank but a band, such as the top quarter of the marks. **NTILE(n)** deals the ordered rows into n buckets and numbers them 1 to n, with bucket sizes as equal as the number of rows allows. When the rows do not divide exactly, **the earlier buckets take the extra rows**.
Four buckets for ten rows give sizes of 3, 3, 2 and 2, because the two rows over go to the first two buckets.

afterFigure.text: A bucket number is a label for a band, and the buckets are equal in the number of rows and *not* in the width of the values they hold.

queries.label: Four buckets
queries.sql: SELECT id, pupil, score, NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS bucket FROM marks ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Three buckets
queries.sql: SELECT id, pupil, score, NTILE(3) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS bucket FROM marks ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Two buckets
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, NTILE(2) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS bucket FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Three buckets
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, NTILE(3) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS bucket FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY id;

lead.text: Numbering the pupils within each class is half of a common task, the other half being to keep only the top one in each. A condition such as `position = 1` cannot go straight into the `WHERE` clause of the same query, because **WHERE is applied before the window functions are calculated**, and the column called `position` does *not* exist yet.

The way round it is to put the numbering in a [[subquery|A SELECT written inside brackets within another query. Met in 'Use one query to define another'.]] and filter in the query that surrounds it. The inner query produces the numbered rows, as in the first query of the figure, and the outer query keeps those whose `position` is 1, as in the second.

afterFigure.text: The outer query reads the inner result as if it were a table. This pattern, **number the rows within each group and then keep the first**, is the standard way to pick one row from each group while keeping the row's other columns.

queries.label: Every pupil numbered
queries.sql: SELECT name, class, score, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY class ORDER BY score DESC) AS position FROM pupils ORDER BY class, position;

queries.label: The top pupil in each class
queries.sql: SELECT name, class, score FROM (SELECT name, class, score, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY class ORDER BY score DESC) AS position FROM pupils) WHERE position = 1 ORDER BY class;

queries.label: Every order numbered
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY id) AS position FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Each customer's first order
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, position FROM (SELECT id, customer_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY id) AS position FROM orders) WHERE position = 1 ORDER BY id;

lessons.orientation: Use PARTITION BY to give each group its own window, and filter the numbers a window produces.
lessons.reviewLabel: Choose which rows a window sees
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: `GROUP BY` gives each customer a total, but the orders themselves disappear into it. To say what share of its customer's spending each order is, a row needs its own amount and its customer's total side by side.
A window function can, once it is told **which rows a calculation sees**, so that each order carries its customer's total beside its own amount.

intro.promise: By the end you'll attach a group's total to each of its rows, restart a numbering for every group, split rows into buckets with NTILE, and keep the first row of each group.

recap.keyIdea: `PARTITION BY` gives each group its own window so that a calculation restarts for every group and every row is kept, and a window value is filtered by wrapping the query.

blocks.text: A window function reads only the rows of its own partition, so `SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id)` writes each customer's total on every one of that customer's rows. The `ORDER BY` inside `OVER` sets the order within a window, and **PARTITION BY** decides which rows share one.

**NTILE(n)** deals ordered rows into n buckets of nearly equal size, with spare rows going to the earlier ones. A window value does *not* exist when `WHERE` runs, so to keep `position = 1` you number the rows in an inner query and filter in the one around it.

recap.nextHook: A window so far has been a whole group. Next you'll let it shrink to the rows up to the current one for running totals, and look at the rows before and after with LAG and LEAD.

lessons.title: Read the rows before and after

lead.text: `SUM(amount) OVER ()` writes the same total, 50, on each of four deposits in a savings jar, because the window is the whole table. A balance that grows with each deposit needs only the rows *up to the current one*.

A **frame** is the part of the window that a function may use for the current row, and it is set after the ordering. The clause `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` says that the frame begins at the first row and ends at the current one. Summed over that frame, the amounts give a **running total**: 20 after the first deposit, 25 after the second, and 50 after the last.

afterFigure.text: Each row therefore has its own frame, and the last row's frame is the whole table, which is why the final running total equals the grand total.

queries.label: The whole total on every row
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, SUM(amount) OVER () AS total FROM jar ORDER BY id;

queries.label: The total so far
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS total FROM jar ORDER BY id;

queries.label: The grand total on every row
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, SUM(amount) OVER () AS total FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: The running total
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS total FROM orders ORDER BY id;

lead.text: When the jar's deposits are ordered by day, two of them fall on day 2. The first query orders by day and then by id, so each row is placed distinctly, and its `ROWS` frame ends *exactly* at the current row. The totals are 20, 25, 40 and 50, one more row at a time.

The second query orders by day alone and uses **RANGE**, which ends the frame at the last row that has the same ordering value as the current row. Rows with the same value are called **peers**, and a `RANGE` frame includes all of them at once. The two deposits on day 2 are peers, so both show the total 40, which is the sum through the end of that day.

afterFigure.text: This is not a rarity. When `ORDER BY` is given and the frame is left unstated, SQLite uses **RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW**, so a running total ordered by a column that repeats will show equal totals for tied rows unless `ROWS` is written, or a unique column is added.

queries.label: ROWS, one row at a time
queries.sql: SELECT id, day, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day, id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS total FROM jar ORDER BY day, id;

queries.label: RANGE, peers together
queries.sql: SELECT id, day, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS total FROM jar ORDER BY day, id;

queries.label: ROWS frame
queries.sql: SELECT id, day, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day, id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS total FROM orders ORDER BY day, id;

queries.label: RANGE frame
queries.sql: SELECT id, day, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS total FROM orders ORDER BY day, id;

lead.text: Often the question is how a row compares with its neighbour, such as today's deposit against yesterday's. **LAG(amount)** returns the amount from the row before the current one in the window's order, and the first row has no row before it, so its value is [[NULL|A marker for a value that is missing or unknown, not the same as zero. Met in 'Know what a row represents'.]].

The word before refers to the order given inside `OVER`, and *not* to how the rows happen to be stored. Deposit 3, of 15, is preceded by the deposit of 5 when the deposits are read in increasing id order and by the deposit of 10 in decreasing order.

afterFigure.text: **Reversing the ordering reverses what before means**, so the ordering should always be written out.

queries.label: Reading forwards
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id ASC) AS previous FROM jar ORDER BY id ASC;

queries.label: Reading backwards
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id DESC) AS previous FROM jar ORDER BY id DESC;

queries.label: Previous in increasing id order
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id ASC) AS previous FROM orders ORDER BY id ASC;

queries.label: Previous in decreasing id order
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id DESC) AS previous FROM orders ORDER BY id DESC;

lead.text: **LEAD** is the mirror image of `LAG`: it returns the value from the next row in the window's order. Like `LAG`, it gives `NULL` when there is no such row, which happens at the last row.

**That NULL is ambiguous**, as the figure shows with a water meter whose second reading is missing. In the first query, the first reading has a next row, but the next reading is *itself* missing, so `LEAD(litres)` returns `NULL` there, and the last reading returns `NULL` because nothing follows it. The second query asks for the next id instead, and it separates the two causes: the first row has a next id of 2, and only the last row has none.

afterFigure.text: When a `NULL` from `LAG` or `LEAD` matters, **check a column that is never missing**, such as the id, to learn whether the neighbour exists.

queries.label: The next reading
queries.sql: SELECT id, litres, LEAD(litres) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS next_litres FROM meter ORDER BY id;

queries.label: The next id
queries.sql: SELECT id, litres, LEAD(id) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS next_id FROM meter ORDER BY id;

queries.label: The next amount
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, LEAD(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS next_amount FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: The next id
queries.sql: SELECT id, LEAD(id) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS next_id FROM orders ORDER BY id;

lessons.orientation: Use window frames for running totals and LAG and LEAD for neighbouring rows, with an explicit ordering.
lessons.reviewLabel: Read the rows before and after
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: The known amounts in the `orders` table add up to 240, but taken in order of id, the same amounts can give **a total that grows order by order**, and beside each order the amount of the order before it, which shows whether sales are *rising* or *falling*.
Both calculations depend on order, so each has to say which row comes first and how far along that order it may look.

intro.promise: By the end you'll write a running total, say how a RANGE frame treats rows that tie, and read the rows before and after the current one with LAG and LEAD.

recap.keyIdea: A frame limits a window to the rows up to the current one, a `RANGE` frame includes tied rows, and `LAG` and `LEAD` read neighbouring rows in an explicit order.

blocks.text: A **frame** chooses which rows of the window a function uses for each row, so `SUM` over `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` gives a running total. A **RANGE** frame includes every row that ties with the current one, so rows that tie in the ordering show the same total.

**LAG** and **LEAD** read the value from the previous and next row in the ordering inside `OVER`, and the ordering must be *written out* for them to mean anything. A `NULL` from either one can mean that there is no neighbouring row or that the neighbour's value is missing, so a column that is never `NULL` is needed to tell the two apart.

questions.prompt: Cy, who is already a customer, places another order. Which table gains a new row?
hints: Ask what one row of each table stands for, and which of those things the purchase has just created.
Cy is already in `customers`, so ask whether the purchase tells the database anything new about Cy.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `orders`

questions.onCorrect: A new order is a new thing of the kind that orders records, so orders gains a row, while Cy's row in customers already exists and nothing about it changes.

misconceptions.feedback: Cy already has a row in `customers`, and nothing about Cy has changed. Ask what the purchase has just created.
A table gains a row only when something new of the kind it records appears. Cy is not new, so one of the two tables stays as it was.

questions.prompt: How many rows of `orders` have `customer_id = 1`?
hints: Read down the `customer_id` column of `orders` and look for the value 1.
Each row that holds a 1 there is one order placed by Ada.
Count those rows rather than counting Ada.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Orders 101 and 102 reference customer 1; there are two.

questions.onCorrect: Orders 101 and 102 both carry Ada's id, so two rows refer to her.

misconceptions.feedback: Ada is one customer, but the question counts rows in orders, and every order she placed has a row of its own.

questions.prompt: The amount of order 106 is unknown. Which value records that in the table?
hints: One of these says that the order cost nothing, which is a claim about the price.
Ask what `SUM` and `AVG` would do with each of these values, and which of them they could skip.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `NULL`

questions.onCorrect: `NULL` marks a value as missing, whereas 0 would claim a price of nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: A zero is a number, and storing it would claim that the order cost nothing. Unknown and zero are different facts.
`'unknown'` is a piece of text sitting where an amount belongs, and `COUNT` and `AVG` would treat it as a known value. A missing amount needs something that is no value at all.

questions.prompt: The shop's customers table holds Ada, Ben, Cy and Dee. Elm signs up and has not ordered anything yet. How many rows does customers hold now?
hints: Elm is a person, so Elm gets a row in the table of people.
Having no orders does not stop Elm from having a customer row.
Add Elm's row to the rows already in customers.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The four original customers plus Elm make five customer rows.

questions.onCorrect: Elm adds one row to customers, which makes five, and nothing to orders until an order is placed.

misconceptions.feedback: Those are the customers before Elm signed up. A new customer gets a row as soon as they sign up, whether or not they have ordered.

questions.prompt: Three customers each place two orders, and the table has one row for each order. How many rows does it hold?
hints: Each order is a row.
Count the orders in total, not the customers.
Each of the three customers places two orders, so add the orders customer by customer.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three customers times two orders each makes six order rows.

questions.onCorrect: Three customers with two orders each place 6 orders, so the table has 6 rows.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the customers. The table has a row for each order, and each customer placed two.
The orders are added up as three groups of two, which is a multiplication.

questions.prompt: Which column can repeat without making an order ambiguous?
hints: An order id has to name one order. Which column has to stay different in every row?
Picture a customer who places two orders and compare the two rows that result.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: orders.customer_id can repeat because one customer can place several orders. The separate order id still identifies each order uniquely.

questions.onCorrect: `customer_id` repeats whenever a customer places several orders, while the order id still names exactly one order.

misconceptions.feedback: The primary key must stay different in every row, because it is the value that names one order.
A column that refers to another table may repeat, as one customer can place several orders.

questions.prompt: How many columns does `SELECT id, amount FROM orders` return?
hints: Count the names between `SELECT` and `FROM`.
Each name gives one column of the result.
The table has more columns than the result does.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The `SELECT` list names `id` and `amount`: two columns.

questions.onCorrect: The `SELECT` list names two columns, so the result has two, however many the table stores.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how many columns the stored `orders` table has. A result contains only the columns its `SELECT` list names.
Look at the `SELECT` list again. It holds a name for each column returned, and there is more than one.

questions.prompt: A query contains amount AS price. What does the AS part change?
hints: Think about where the name price can be seen.
The stored table keeps its own column names.

acceptedIdeas: The heading in the query result
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: AS price labels the column in this query's result. It does not rename the stored amount column.

choices.label: The heading in the query result

questions.onCorrect: AS names the column in the result, so the stored column and its values stay as they were.

misconceptions.feedback: The alias works on the result only. The stored values are read as they are and are not altered by a query.
AS has nothing to do with which rows are read. It only gives a column of the result another name.

questions.prompt: A query works out `amount * 2` for every order. What does it give for order 101, whose amount is 80?
hints: The star between two values is multiplication.
Order 101 has an amount of 80.
Multiply that amount by the number after the star.
questions.onCorrect: The expression is worked out for the row, so 80 multiplied by 2 gives 160.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 2 to the amount. The star is the multiplication sign, so the amount is multiplied by 2.
That halves the amount, which is what the division in the figure did. This expression multiplies.

questions.prompt: A query works out amount + 10 for every order. What does it give for order 102, whose amount is 20?
hints: The plus sign adds.
Order 102 has an amount of 20.
Add the number after the plus sign to that amount.
questions.onCorrect: The expression adds 10 to the amount of the row, so 20 and 10 give 30.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the two numbers. The plus sign adds them.
That is the stored amount. The expression adds a further 10 to it in the result.

questions.prompt: An amount is 15. What would `SELECT amount * 3 AS tripled` return for that row?
hints: The alias only names the column.
The star multiplies the amount.
Multiply the amount by 3.
questions.onCorrect: The expression is 15 multiplied by 3, which is 45, and tripled is only its heading.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 3 to the amount. The star between them means multiplication.
That divides the amount by 3. The star multiplies.

questions.prompt: After `SELECT amount AS price FROM orders`, what is the column called in the stored `orders` table?
hints: The alias exists only in the result.
Which name did the stored table use before the query ran?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `amount`

choices.label: Both names, the old one and the new one

questions.onCorrect: The stored column is still called amount, because price names the result column only.

misconceptions.feedback: The alias `price` appears in the result only. The stored table keeps its original column name.
An alias names the column in the result only. It does not add a second name to the stored table.

questions.prompt: How many orders satisfy `amount >= 40`?
hints: Test the amount of each order against the limit.
An amount of exactly 40 passes the symbol `>=`.
An order with no amount cannot be shown to pass.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Orders 101, 103 and 104 satisfy the comparison; 106 has a missing amount.

questions.onCorrect: Orders 101, 103 and 104 have amounts of 80, 80 and 40, and the missing amount of order 106 fails the test.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the order whose amount is exactly on the limit. The symbol `>=` keeps a row that equals it.
The unknown amount of order 106 cannot be shown to reach the limit, so that row is not kept.

questions.prompt: How many orders satisfy `status = 'paid' AND amount >= 40`?
hints: `AND` needs both conditions to be true for the same order.
First list the orders that are paid.
Of those, keep the ones whose amount reaches the limit.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only paid orders 101 and 103 also have amount at least 40.

questions.onCorrect: Only orders 101 and 103 are both paid and worth at least 40.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every order whose amount reaches the limit, including one that is still pending. The status has to match as well.
That is the count when either condition is enough, as with `OR`. `AND` needs both.

questions.prompt: Which values can pass `amount BETWEEN 20 AND 40`?
hints: `BETWEEN` is shorthand for two comparisons joined by `AND`.
Ask whether a value of exactly 20, or of exactly 40, passes those comparisons.

acceptedIdeas: Values from 20 to 40, with both ends included
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Values from 20 to 40, with both ends included

choices.label: Values from 20 to 40, with both ends excluded
Values from 20 to 40, with only the lower end included
Values from 20 to 40, with both ends included

questions.onCorrect: `BETWEEN` counts both ends, so every value from 20 up to and including 40 passes.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the reading of a pair of strict comparisons, greater than 20 and less than 40. `BETWEEN` is not written with strict ones.
`BETWEEN` has no special rule for one end. Both limits are handled the same way.

questions.prompt: How many orders have `item IN ('Book', 'Lamp')`?
hints: IN is true when the item matches any value in the list.
Count the orders for each of the two items.
Add the two counts. The condition looks at the item only.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two Book orders and two Lamp orders make four.

questions.onCorrect: Two orders are books and two are lamps, and order 106 counts because the condition never reads its missing amount.

misconceptions.feedback: Order 106 is a lamp, and the condition tests only the item, so a missing amount does not remove it.
The list names two of the three items. The desk orders are not in it.

questions.prompt: The shop's six orders have the amounts 80, 20, 80, 40, 20 and `NULL`. How many orders satisfy `amount > 20 AND amount < 80`?
hints: Both symbols are strict, so the limits themselves do not pass.
Look for amounts that lie between the two limits.
A missing amount cannot pass either comparison.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only the amount 40 lies strictly between 20 and 80. The 20s and 80s sit on the limits, and the `NULL` passes neither comparison.

questions.onCorrect: Only the amount of 40 lies strictly between 20 and 80.

misconceptions.feedback: The limits do not count under strict symbols, so check which amounts really lie between them.
Neither 20 nor 80 passes a strict comparison, so look again at the amounts that remain.

questions.prompt: Which condition finds an unknown amount?
hints: A comparison with an unknown value is itself unknown.
SQL has its own wording for asking whether a value is missing.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Use amount IS NULL to test for a missing value. Equality to NULL does not evaluate to true in SQL.

questions.onCorrect: `IS NULL` asks whether the value is missing, which a comparison cannot do.

misconceptions.feedback: Comparing with `NULL` gives unknown for every row, so the condition keeps nothing. A missing value is asked for with `IS NULL`.
Zero is a stored number, and a missing amount is not a zero. The two are different facts.

questions.prompt: Which part of the query promises that the orders arrive in increasing order of id?
hints: Which part of a query is written to state an order?
A table can hand its rows back in whatever order is convenient unless the query says otherwise.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: ORDER BY id ASC explicitly requests increasing ids. Without ORDER BY, the query makes no promise about the order of its result rows.

questions.onCorrect: Only `ORDER BY` makes a promise about order, whatever the table's layout happens to be.

misconceptions.feedback: The way rows happen to be stored may change, so it is not something a query can rely on.
`SELECT *` chooses columns and says nothing about the order of the rows.

questions.prompt: With `ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC` over the known amounts, which id appears first?
hints: `DESC` puts the largest amount first.
Two orders share the largest amount, so the tie-breaker decides between them.
`id ASC` puts the smaller id first.

hints: First find the North customers.
Their ids form the list for IN.
Count the orders whose customer id is on that list.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Customers 1 and 3 are North; each has two orders.

questions.onCorrect: Ada and Cy are in the North, and they placed two orders each.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the North customers. The result has a row for every order they placed.
Order 106 belongs to a North customer, and the condition tests the customer id, not the amount.

questions.prompt: Why does `EXISTS` return Ada once even though she has two orders?
hints: `EXISTS` gives a yes or a no for the row it is examining.
Ask how many times the outer query reads Ada's row in `customers`.

acceptedIdeas: The outer query reads one row for each customer
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The outer query reads one row for each customer

choices.label: The outer query reads one row for each customer
`EXISTS` returns only the first matching order

questions.onCorrect: The outer query reads each customer once, and `EXISTS` only decides whether that row is kept.

misconceptions.feedback: `EXISTS` removes nothing. It gives a yes or a no for the row being examined, and Ada's row is examined once.
`EXISTS` does not return orders at all. The rows in the result are customers.

questions.prompt: How many orders are strictly above the average for their own item?
hints: Find the average amount for each item.
Compare each order with the average of its own item.
Check whether any order is larger than its item's average.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Desk amounts equal 80, Book amounts equal 20 and Lamp's known amount equals 40; each equals its item average.

questions.onCorrect: Orders for the same item have equal amounts, so none is above its own item's average.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count against the overall average. Here each order is compared with its own item's average.
Compare the orders for each item with that item's own average. None of them exceeds it.

questions.prompt: Three customers have zero, one and four orders. How many customers pass `EXISTS` for an order?
hints: `EXISTS` is true when the inner query finds at least one row.
A customer with no orders finds none.
Count the customers with at least one order.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two customers have at least one order; the number of matches does not duplicate them.

questions.onCorrect: The customers with one and with four orders each have at least one order, and the first customer has none.

misconceptions.feedback: The customer with no orders finds no row in the subquery, so `EXISTS` is false for that customer.
`EXISTS` counts customers who have an order, not the orders themselves.

questions.prompt: What is the term for a subquery that refers to a value from the current outer row?
hints: The subquery's result depends on the outer row.
The word describes how the two queries are related.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A correlated subquery uses a value from the current outer row. Its meaning depends on which outer row is being considered.

questions.onCorrect: A subquery that uses a value from the outer row is called correlated.

misconceptions.feedback: A scalar subquery returns a single value, whether or not it uses the outer row. The word needed describes the link between the two queries.

questions.prompt: How does `UNION` combine its inputs?
hints: `UNION` combines results vertically; `JOIN` matches related rows.
Ask whether `UNION` needs any key to line two results up, or only rows of a compatible shape.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: UNION stacks compatible rows from its SELECT results and removes duplicates. It combines rows vertically rather than matching columns through a join.

choices.label: It changes the stored table names
It matches customer keys to order keys

questions.onCorrect: It stacks compatible result rows. A join, by contrast, matches related rows.

misconceptions.feedback: Matching keys is what `JOIN` does. `UNION` stacks results.
`UNION` only combines results. It never touches stored tables.

questions.prompt: One query selects the ids of the paid orders, and another selects the ids of the orders worth at least 40. How many rows does the `UNION` of the two queries return?
hints: `UNION` keeps an id that is on both lists once.
List the ids from the two results.
Cross out each id that appears twice and count the rest.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The unique ids are 101, 102, 103, 104 and 105.

questions.onCorrect: The ids 101, 102, 103, 104 and 105 are on the lists, and 101 and 103 are on both but counted once.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count for `UNION ALL`, which keeps the orders on both lists twice. `UNION` keeps each once.
Some ids are on only one of the two lists, and `UNION` keeps those too.

questions.prompt: The paid-ids query and the at-least-40 query now each also select a label, `'paid'` for the first and `'large'` for the second. How many rows does their `UNION` return?
hints: `UNION` compares whole rows, including the label.
An order on both lists now has a different label on each.
Add the rows of the two labelled results.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The four paid rows and three large rows have different labels, so all seven full rows are distinct.

questions.onCorrect: The labels make an order that is on both lists into two different rows, so no row is removed.

misconceptions.feedback: That would be the count without the labels. With a different label on each row, an order on both lists is no longer a repeat.

questions.prompt: The paid-ids query `UNION` the at-least-40 query is sorted by id, smallest first. What is the third id in the sorted list?
hints: Stack the two lists and remove the repeated ids.
Sort the ids from smallest to largest.
Read down to the third row.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The ordered unique ids start 101, 102, 103.

questions.onCorrect: The sorted list begins 101, 102, 103, so the third id is the third different one.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the repeated 101 twice. `UNION` keeps it once, so the third row is the next id along.
Check the order of the list again, as an id has been counted that comes later.

questions.prompt: Query A returns ids 1, 2, 3. Query B returns 2, 4. How many rows does `UNION ALL` return?
hints: `UNION ALL` removes nothing.
Count the rows of each result.
Add the two counts.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: `UNION ALL` retains all three rows from A and both rows from B: five.

questions.onCorrect: `UNION ALL` keeps every row of both results, so the three rows and the two rows make five.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count for `UNION`, which removes the repeated 2. `UNION ALL` keeps it.
`UNION ALL` stacks both results, so the rows of the second are added to those of the first.

questions.prompt: Which requirement applies to the `SELECT` results combined by `UNION`?
hints: The results are stacked, so their shapes must fit.
Ask what a row of one result and a row of the other have to share to sit in the same column positions.

acceptedIdeas: They must have the same number of result columns
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each SELECT must return the same number of columns, with corresponding columns representing compatible values. UNION aligns columns by position, not by name.

choices.label: Both queries must read their rows from the same table
They must have the same number of result columns
The columns of both must have the same names

questions.onCorrect: Stacked rows must line up, so each `SELECT` returns the same number of columns.

misconceptions.feedback: Each part can read any table, since a union simply stacks whatever the parts return.
`UNION` takes its column names from the first `SELECT`, so the names in the other can differ. What has to match is the number of columns.

questions.prompt: What does a window calculation preserve here?
hints: Compare the five-row window result with the grouped result.
A grouped result has fewer rows than the table it came from. Ask whether the window result does.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A window calculation adds a result to each retained order row. Unlike GROUP BY aggregation, it does not collapse the rows into one row per group.

choices.label: One row for each different amount

questions.onCorrect: Each individual known order row. A window calculation adds a value without collapsing rows.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what `GROUP BY` does, one row for each group. A window calculation keeps every row.
Nothing is filtered out. Every known order stays.

questions.prompt: The shop's known order amounts are 80, 20, 80, 40 and 20. Under `RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC)`, what rank does the amount 40 receive?
hints: The two amounts of 80 tie for the first rank.
`RANK` counts the rows ahead of this one.
Add one to the number of rows ahead of the amount 40.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two 80 rows share rank 1, so the next row's rank is 3.

questions.onCorrect: Two orders are ahead of the amount 40, so `RANK` gives it the next number after them.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the different amounts ahead, which is what `DENSE_RANK` does. `RANK` counts the rows ahead.
Only the rows ahead of the amount count, and the two amounts of 20 come after it.

questions.prompt: The shop's known order amounts are 80, 20, 80, 40 and 20. Under `DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC)`, what rank does the amount 40 receive?
hints: `DENSE_RANK` counts different amounts, not rows.
How many different amounts are larger than 40?
Add one to that number.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 80 is the first distinct amount; 40 is the second.

questions.onCorrect: Only one different amount, 80, is ahead of 40, so its dense rank is the next whole number.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the rank `RANK` gives, which leaves a gap after the tie. `DENSE_RANK` does not skip numbers.
Only different amounts ahead of 40 count, and both amounts of 80 are one value.

questions.prompt: On the shop's amounts, orders 101 and 103 tie at 80. What happens to that tie if `id` is added inside the ranking window's `ORDER BY`?
hints: Rows tie only if they are equal in every `ORDER BY` column.
Compare the ids of the two orders.

acceptedIdeas: The two rows no longer tie
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Window ties depend on every ORDER BY expression. Adding distinct ids makes the two 80 rows different ordering keys, so they no longer tie.

choices.label: Both rows must still have rank 1
The two rows no longer tie

questions.onCorrect: The two orders have different ids, so they are no longer equal in the ordering and receive different ranks.

misconceptions.feedback: Rows share a rank only if they are equal in every ordering column. Their ids differ, so the tie is broken.
A ranking window changes nothing in the table. It only changes the column of ranks in the result.

questions.prompt: Amounts sorted descending are 90, 90, 70, 50. What is `RANK` for 70?
hints: The two amounts of 90 tie for first.
`RANK` counts the rows ahead of this one.
Add one to the number of rows ahead of 70.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two higher rows precede 70, so its ordinary rank is 3.

questions.onCorrect: Two rows are ahead of 70, so `RANK` gives it the third place, with a gap after the tie.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the dense rank, which counts different values. `RANK` counts the rows ahead.
Only the rows ahead of 70 count, and the amount of 50 comes after it.

questions.prompt: Type the name of the window function that gives every row its own position, even when two rows are equal in the ordering.
hints: This function numbers the rows one by one.
It does not share positions between rows that tie.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: ROW_NUMBER

questions.onCorrect: `ROW_NUMBER` gives each row its own number, even when two rows are equal in the ordering.

misconceptions.feedback: That function lets tied rows share a position. The one wanted gives every row its own number.

questions.prompt: With `PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY id`, what `ROW_NUMBER` does order 103 get?
hints: Order 103 belongs to customer 2.
Numbering starts again at the beginning of each customer.
Where does order 103 sit among customer 2's orders?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 103 is customer 2's first order, so its position in that customer's window is 1.

questions.onCorrect: Order 103 is the first order of customer 2, and the numbering starts again for each customer.

misconceptions.feedback: That is its position among all the orders. `PARTITION BY` restarts the numbering for each customer.
Order 104 is the second order of that customer. Order 103 comes first.

questions.prompt: What total does `SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY status)` attach to every paid order?
hints: The window holds all the orders that share the status.
Find the paid orders and their amounts.
Add the known amounts.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The paid amounts are 80, 20, 80 and 20, totalling 200.

questions.onCorrect: The four paid orders add up to 200, and the total is written beside each of them.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds every order, pending ones included. The paid window holds only the paid orders.
That is the total of the pending window. The question is about the paid orders.

questions.prompt: With `NTILE(3)` over five known-amount orders ordered by id, how many rows are in bucket 1?
hints: Five rows divide into three buckets with two rows over.
The earlier buckets take the extra rows.
How many extra rows does bucket 1 receive?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Five rows split into buckets of 2, 2 and 1; the first bucket contains two.

questions.onCorrect: Five rows give buckets of 2, 2 and 1, because the spare rows go to the earlier buckets.

misconceptions.feedback: The first bucket takes one of the spare rows, so it is larger than the last one.
A bucket takes at most one spare row, and with five rows it cannot hold that many.

questions.prompt: You have numbered each customer's orders with `ROW_NUMBER` and want only the rows numbered 1. How do you filter to `position = 1` in SQLite?
hints: `WHERE` is applied before window functions are calculated.
The numbers must exist before the filter can read them.

acceptedIdeas: Use an outer query over the numbered result
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Compute ROW_NUMBER in an inner query or CTE, then filter position = 1 in the outer query. SQLite cannot use that window result in the same SELECT's WHERE clause.

choices.label: Put the window function directly in the same query's `WHERE`
Use an outer query over the numbered result

questions.onCorrect: Put the numbered query inside an outer query, which can then keep `position = 1`.

misconceptions.feedback: `WHERE` is applied before the window functions are calculated, so the number does not exist at that point.
Renaming ids would damage the data, and the numbering would not change. The filter has to read the computed position.

questions.prompt: Seven rows are distributed by `NTILE(3)`. How many rows are in the first bucket?
hints: Seven rows divide into three buckets with one row over.
The earlier buckets take the extra rows.
Work out how many rows each bucket holds, starting with the first.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The three bucket sizes are 3, 2 and 2; the first bucket holds three.

questions.onCorrect: Seven rows give buckets of 3, 2 and 2, with the one spare row going to the first bucket.

misconceptions.feedback: Seven rows do not divide evenly into three buckets, and the spare row goes to the first one.
Only one row is left over, so the first bucket cannot take more than a single extra one.

questions.prompt: What does `PARTITION BY` change?
hints: It divides the rows into separate groups.
Compare it with `GROUP BY` and ask whether every row still appears in the result.

acceptedIdeas: Which rows each calculation looks at together
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Which rows each calculation looks at together

choices.label: Which rows each calculation looks at together
How many rows come back, one for each partition
The order in which the rows are listed

questions.onCorrect: `PARTITION BY` decides which rows belong together in each calculation window, while every row stays in the result.

misconceptions.feedback: `PARTITION BY` keeps every row. That is the difference from `GROUP BY`, which returns one row for each group.
The order inside each window comes from the `ORDER BY` after `OVER`. `PARTITION BY` only decides which rows belong together.

questions.prompt: Taking the shop's orders in increasing id order, what is the running total of the known amounts at order 103?
hints: The running total includes orders 101, 102 and 103.
Add their known amounts.
Orders after 103 are not in the frame yet.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Orders 101, 102 and 103 contribute 80 + 20 + 80 = 180.

questions.onCorrect: The amounts 80, 20 and 80 of orders 101 to 103 add up to 180.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the grand total, which includes the orders after 103. The running total stops at the current row.
That is the running total at order 102. Order 103 adds its own amount.

questions.prompt: The shop's orders are summed with a `RANGE` frame ordered by day, and orders 102 and 103 were both placed on 2 September. Why do both rows show the same total?
hints: `RANGE` treats rows with the same ordering value as peers.
Ask which rows the frame of order 102 includes.

acceptedIdeas: The frame includes both rows with the same day
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The RANGE frame includes peers with the same ordering value. Both September 2 rows include the whole day and share its cumulative total of 180.

choices.label: `SUM` over a window always returns the grand total
The frame includes both rows with the same day
The two orders are merged into a single row

questions.onCorrect: The two orders are peers on the same day, and a `RANGE` frame includes all peers, so each row's frame ends at the same place.

misconceptions.feedback: A `SUM` with a frame covers only the rows in that frame. These totals still grow down the list.
Both orders still appear as separate rows. Each shows 180 because the frame of each reaches the same last row, which is order 103.

questions.prompt: With increasing ids, what does `LAG(amount)` return at order 104?
hints: `LAG` reads the row before the current one.
Which order comes just before 104 in increasing id order?
Read that order's amount.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The preceding row is order 103, whose amount is 80.

questions.onCorrect: Order 103 comes just before order 104, and `LAG` returns its amount.

misconceptions.feedback: That is order 104's own amount. `LAG` reads the row before it.
That is the amount two rows back. `LAG` reads the row immediately before.

questions.prompt: With increasing ids, what does `LEAD(amount)` return at order 103?
hints: `LEAD` reads the row after the current one.
Which order comes just after 103 in increasing id order?
Read that order's amount.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The next row is order 104, whose amount is 40.

questions.onCorrect: Order 104 comes just after order 103, and `LEAD` returns its amount.

misconceptions.feedback: That is order 103's own amount. `LEAD` reads the row after it.
That is the amount of the row before, which `LAG` would give. `LEAD` looks forwards.

questions.prompt: Ordered amounts are 10, `NULL` and 30. What is the running `SUM` at the third row?
hints: The running sum includes every row up to the third.
`SUM` skips the `NULL`.
Add the known amounts.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The known contributing amounts are 10 and 30. Their running sum is 40.

questions.onCorrect: The frame holds 10, `NULL` and 30, and `SUM` skips the `NULL`, which leaves 40.

misconceptions.feedback: The running sum at the third row includes the earlier rows as well as the third one.
That is the running sum at the first and second rows. The third row adds its own amount.

questions.prompt: A `LEAD(amount)` value is `NULL`. What can you conclude from that value alone?
hints: There are two ways for `LEAD` to give `NULL`.
Think about the last row, and about a next row whose amount is missing.

acceptedIdeas: Either there is no next row or its amount is missing
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Either there is no next row or its amount is missing

choices.label: There is definitely no row after the current one
There is a next row, and its amount is missing
There is a next row, and its amount is zero
Either there is no next row or its amount is missing

questions.onCorrect: `LEAD` gives `NULL` when no row follows and also when the next row's amount is itself `NULL`.

misconceptions.feedback: A next row can exist and still give `NULL`, if its own amount is missing.
`LEAD` also gives `NULL` at the last row, where nothing follows, so the value alone cannot show that a next row exists.
A zero is a stored number, and `LEAD` would return it as 0. `NULL` is not a number.

questions.prompt: Four pupils were asked how many books they read this month. Three answered 4, 6 and 8. The fourth left the box empty. What is the average of the answers?
hints: `AVG` skips the missing answer.
Add the three known answers and divide by how many there are.
Add the three answers first.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The answers are 4, 6 and 8. They add up to 18, and 18 ÷ 3 = 6.

questions.onCorrect: The three answers add to 18, and dividing by the three known answers gives 6.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by all four pupils, including the one who did not answer. `AVG` divides by the number of known answers.
That is the total of the answers. An average divides the total by how many answers there are.

questions.prompt: Which one counts every row, including rows with an unknown amount?
hints: Which one does not look at a single column?
Putting a column inside the brackets makes the function look at that column's known values only.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: COUNT(*) counts rows. COUNT(amount) counts only rows where amount is known.

questions.onCorrect: `COUNT(*)` counts rows. Counting a column counts only its known values.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts known amounts only, so a row with an unknown amount is left out.
`SUM` adds amounts. It does not count rows.

questions.prompt: Why does `AVG(amount)` divide by one here, not two?
hints: How many of the two amounts are known?
`AVG` is a sum divided by a count, so ask which values each of those two parts includes.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: One of the two amounts is unknown, and AVG leaves it out of both the sum and the count.

choices.label: `AVG` treats the unknown amount as zero.

questions.onCorrect: `AVG` skips unknown values in the sum and in the count, so it divides by the known amounts only.

misconceptions.feedback: Then it would divide by both orders. `AVG` skips unknown values instead.
Nothing says it was cancelled. Its amount is simply not known.

questions.prompt: A column holds 5, `NULL`, 7 and 8. What does `COUNT(column)` return?
hints: `COUNT(column)` counts rows where the column has a value.
A `NULL` cell has no value.
Set the `NULL` aside and count the cells that remain.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three of the four values are known, so `COUNT(column)` is three.

questions.onCorrect: Three cells hold a value, and `COUNT(column)` skips the `NULL`.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of rows, which `COUNT(*)` would return. `COUNT(column)` skips the `NULL`.

questions.prompt: Six pupils score 10, 50, 60, 70, 80 and 90, and everyone above the class average gets a sticker. How many pupils get a sticker?
hints: Find the class average first: add the scores and divide by the number of pupils.
Compare each score with the average.
A score equal to the average is not above it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The scores add up to 360, so the average is 60. The scores above it are 70, 80 and 90.

questions.onCorrect: The scores add to 360, so the average is 60, and only 70, 80 and 90 are above it.

misconceptions.feedback: The score of 60 equals the average, and 'above' means strictly greater, so that pupil gets no sticker.
The score of 50 is below the average, so that pupil does not get a sticker.

questions.prompt: What does the subquery in `WHERE amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders)` supply?
hints: How many numbers does `AVG` return?
The comparison in `WHERE` needs one thing to set each amount against. Ask what kind of thing `AVG` hands back.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: AVG returns a single number, and the outer condition compares each amount with it.

choices.label: A table of rows to join with

questions.onCorrect: A subquery in parentheses can supply a value or a set to the outer query. Here it supplies one number.

misconceptions.feedback: Here the subquery returns a single number, not rows to join.
A subquery supplies values, not column names.

questions.prompt: Five customers have 0, 2, 0, 0 and 5 orders. How many customers pass `NOT EXISTS` for an order?
hints: `NOT EXISTS` is true when the inner query finds no row.
Which customers have no order at all?
Count them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three customers have no order, so `NOT EXISTS` keeps three.

questions.onCorrect: The three customers with no orders find no row, so `NOT EXISTS` is true for each of them.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the customers who do have orders, which is what `EXISTS` keeps. `NOT EXISTS` keeps the others.
`NOT EXISTS` counts customers, not orders, so the number of orders is not what the test counts.

questions.prompt: Chess club has Ann, Bo, Cy and Di. Drama club has Cy, Di, Ed and Flo. How many names are on a single list of every pupil in either club?
hints: A pupil in both clubs is one person, so the name appears once.
List the names, and cross out the repeats.
Count the names that are left.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Cy and Di are in both clubs. Ann, Bo, Cy, Di, Ed and Flo make six names.

questions.onCorrect: Cy and Di are in both clubs, so the eight names on the two lists make six different pupils.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two lists. Cy and Di are on both, so that sum counts them twice.
That is the size of one club. The list should hold the members of both.

questions.prompt: Query A returns ids 1 and 2. Query B returns ids 2 and 3. How many rows does `A UNION B` return?
hints: Which id is in both results?
`UNION` keeps a repeated row once.
List the different ids and count them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The ids are 1, 2 and 3. The id 2 is in both results, but `UNION` keeps it once.

questions.onCorrect: 3. `UNION` stacks the two results and keeps each different row once.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds both results. The id found in both appears once under `UNION`.

questions.prompt: Why does `UNION ALL` return order 101 twice?
hints: Which of the two results contains 101?
Ask what `UNION ALL` does with a row that turns up in both of the results.

acceptedIdeas: Order 101 is in both results, and `UNION ALL` keeps both.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Order 101 is paid and also at least 40, so both queries return it.

choices.label: Order 101 was paid twice, so the table holds two rows for it.
Order 101 is in both results, and `UNION ALL` keeps both.
`UNION ALL` adds an extra copy of every row it combines.

questions.onCorrect: `UNION ALL` keeps every occurrence, so a row in both results appears twice.

misconceptions.feedback: The table has one row for order 101. Two queries each returned it.
A row repeats only when both queries return it. A row returned by just one query appears once.

questions.prompt: A returns `(1, 'x')` and `(2, 'x')`. B returns `(1, 'y')` and `(2, 'x')`. How many rows does `A UNION B` return?
hints: `UNION` compares whole rows.
Find a row that appears in both results.
Remove the repeat and count the rows that are left.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The row (2, 'x') is in both results and is kept once. (1, 'x') and (1, 'y') are different rows.

questions.onCorrect: Only (2, 'x') is in both results, so the four rows reduce to three.

misconceptions.feedback: The row `(2, 'x')` appears in both results, and `UNION` keeps one copy of it.
`UNION` compares both values of a row, so rows that differ in either value are kept.

questions.prompt: A bakery's till log for the day reads: bun, loaf, bun, roll, bun, bagel, loaf. How many different kinds of bread were sold?
hints: Different kinds means each kind counted once.
List each kind the first time it appears and skip the repeats.
Count the kinds on your list.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The kinds are bun, loaf, roll and bagel, so there are four.

questions.onCorrect: Bun, loaf, roll and bagel make four kinds, however many times each was sold.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every sale. The question asks for the number of different kinds, so each kind counts once.
Check the list again: one kind has been counted twice, and repeats count once.

questions.prompt: `DISTINCT colour, size` is applied to the rows (red, S), (red, M) and (red, S). Which rows come back?
hints: Which rows are exactly the same in both columns?
`DISTINCT` keeps one copy of each set of identical rows and leaves rows that differ alone.

acceptedIdeas: (red, S) and (red, M), one of each
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The two (red, S) rows match completely and collapse into one. (red, M) differs in size and stays.

choices.label: Only (red, S), as every row is red
(red, S) and (red, M), one of each
All three rows, as the sizes differ

questions.onCorrect: `DISTINCT` compares the whole selected row, so only rows that match in every column collapse.

misconceptions.feedback: All three rows share the colour, but `DISTINCT` compares size as well.
Two rows match in both columns, and `DISTINCT` collapses exact repeats.

questions.prompt: The rows (A, x), (A, y), (B, x), (B, y) and (A, x) are selected. How many rows does `SELECT DISTINCT` return?
hints: `DISTINCT` compares both values of a row together.
Look for a row that repeats an earlier row exactly.
Remove the repeat and count what is left.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only (A, x) repeats. Removing the duplicate leaves four rows.

questions.onCorrect: Only (A, x) repeats, so removing the second copy leaves four different rows.

misconceptions.feedback: The last row repeats the first exactly, so `DISTINCT` removes it.
`DISTINCT` compares whole rows, not the first value alone, so rows that differ in either value are kept.

questions.prompt: A bookshop sign says 'Books at least £20'. The shelf holds books priced 5, 12, 20, 25 and 30 pounds. How many books does the sign cover?
hints: 'At least 20' includes 20 itself.
Test each price in turn: does it reach 20?
Count the prices that pass.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At least £20 covers the books at 20, 25 and 30 pounds: three books.

questions.onCorrect: The prices 20, 25 and 30 pass the test, because 'at least' includes the limit.

misconceptions.feedback: A price of exactly 20 is at least 20, so it is covered. 'At least' includes the limit itself.
Some of the prices fall below the limit, so not every book passes the test.

questions.prompt: `WHERE amount > 50` is applied to the amounts 30, 60, `NULL` and 90. Which rows stay?
hints: Which of these amounts are above the line, and what happens to the unknown one?
A `WHERE` condition keeps a row only when it is true. Ask whether comparing an unknown amount with 50 is true.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 60 and 90 are greater than 50. 30 is not, and a comparison with NULL is never true.

questions.onCorrect: 60 and 90. A row stays only when its condition is true, and a comparison with an unknown amount never is.

misconceptions.feedback: An unknown amount cannot be shown to be above 50, so its row is dropped.
60 is above 50 too. Check each amount against the condition.

questions.prompt: A query keeps the orders where `status = 'paid' OR amount >= 40`. Order 102 is paid, and its amount is only 20. Does the query keep order 102?
hints: Check which of the two conditions order 102 passes.
Ask whether `OR` needs one of its conditions to be true or both.

acceptedIdeas: Yes, because it passes one of the two conditions
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes, because it passes one of the two conditions

choices.label: No, because it fails the test on the amount
Yes, because it passes one of the two conditions
No, because `OR` needs both conditions to hold

questions.onCorrect: Order 102 passes `status = 'paid'`, and `OR` needs only one true condition, so the low amount does not remove it.

misconceptions.feedback: A row can fail one condition and still be kept. Check whether order 102 passes the other one.
That describes `AND`, which needs both conditions. The query uses `OR`.

questions.prompt: The amounts are 10, 20, 30, `NULL` and 40. How many pass `amount BETWEEN 20 AND 40`?
hints: `BETWEEN` counts both of its ends.
Check each amount against both limits, and set the `NULL` aside.
Count the amounts that pass.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 20, 30 and 40 pass. 10 is below the range and `NULL` passes nothing.

questions.onCorrect: The amounts 20, 30 and 40 pass, and the `NULL` passes no comparison.

misconceptions.feedback: `BETWEEN` counts both ends, so the amounts that sit on the limits pass as well.
A comparison with the missing value is unknown, so its row is not kept.

questions.prompt: A café's till has three rows: tea 3, coffee 4 and tea 4, with the amounts in pounds. Grouped by drink, how much did tea sell for in total, in pounds?
hints: Each group is built from the rows that share a drink.
Find the rows in the tea group.
Add their amounts.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The tea rows are £3 and £4, which add up to £7.

questions.onCorrect: The tea group holds the rows of 3 and 4 pounds, and its total is 7.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds every row, including the coffee. A group's total uses only the rows in that group.
That is the coffee group's total. The tea group has two rows.

questions.prompt: In a grouped report, one result row stands for what?
hints: Think about what `GROUP BY` gathers.
Compare how many input rows a group covers with how many result rows it produces.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: GROUP BY gathers rows that share a value, and each gathered set becomes one result row.

questions.onCorrect: Each result row of a grouped report stands for a whole group of input rows.

misconceptions.feedback: Grouping gathers several rows together, so a result row stands for many.
Columns are the facts shown. Rows are what the report counts.

questions.prompt: Why does the pending group show fewer known amounts than orders?
hints: Compare `COUNT(*)` with `COUNT(amount)` for the group.
Look at the pending orders in the table and check whether any of them has an unknown amount.

acceptedIdeas: One pending order has no recorded amount.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: COUNT(*) counts both pending orders. COUNT(amount) skips the one whose amount is unknown.

choices.label: One pending order has no recorded amount.
Pending orders are not counted at all.

questions.onCorrect: `COUNT(*)` counts orders and `COUNT(amount)` counts known amounts, so an unknown amount makes them differ.

misconceptions.feedback: `COUNT(*)` counts every row in the group, whatever its values.
Both pending orders are counted in the orders column.

questions.prompt: The rows are tea (paid) 3, tea (pending) 5 and coffee (paid) 4. After `WHERE status = 'paid'` and `GROUP BY item`, what is tea's `SUM`?
hints: `WHERE` is applied before the grouping.
Which tea rows are left after the filter?
Add the amounts of the tea rows that remain.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: `WHERE` removes the pending tea row first, so tea's group holds only the paid 3.

questions.onCorrect: The filter removes the pending tea row, so the tea group holds only the paid row of 3.

misconceptions.feedback: That includes the pending tea row, which `WHERE` removed before the grouping.
The coffee row belongs to a different group, so it does not add to the tea total.

questions.prompt: Each pupil has a club number: Ann 1, Bo 2, Cy 1 and Di 3. Club 1 is Chess. How many pupils would a Chess list show?
hints: Match each pupil's club number against the number of the Chess club.
Check the club number of every pupil in turn.
Count the pupils whose number matches.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Club 1 is Chess. Ann and Cy both have club number 1, so the list shows two pupils.

questions.onCorrect: Ann and Cy both hold club number 1, so two pupils are matched with Chess.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every pupil. Only the pupils whose club number matches Chess are paired with it.
More than one pupil holds the Chess club's number, and each of them is a separate matching pair.

questions.prompt: A pupil row holds `club = 2`. The club ids are 1, 2 and 3. How many club rows does that pupil match in a join on the club number?
hints: Which club id equals the pupil's club number?
Compare the number with each club id in turn.
How many of the club ids are the same number?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only the club row whose id is 2 matches, so the pupil pairs with one club row.

questions.onCorrect: 1. A join pairs a row only with rows whose key value is equal to its own.

misconceptions.feedback: That is every club. The pupil matches only the club with its own number.

questions.prompt: Customers P, Q and R have 3, 1 and 0 orders. How many rows does `SELECT DISTINCT name` over their `INNER JOIN` return?
hints: First decide which customers appear in the joined result.
A customer with no orders forms no pair.
`DISTINCT` keeps each remaining name once.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: P and Q each have orders, so each appears. R has no pair. `DISTINCT` leaves two names.

questions.onCorrect: Only P and Q have orders, and `DISTINCT` keeps each of their names once, whatever the number of pairs.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the matching pairs. `DISTINCT` collapses the repeated names into one row each.
The customer with no orders forms no pair, so that name never reaches the result.

questions.prompt: Class A pupils scored 6 and 8, and class B has one pupil who scored 5. Beside the pupil who scored 6 you write the total for their class. What do you write?
